### Concepts and General Information


##### 1.1. General principles

Standard interfaces are provided in form of SMOG services (xml-files).
To make use of standard interfaces, an implementation project will have to:

* provide updated SMOG xml-files for custom attributes and mappings (if any)
* use the ioservice\_builder tool to generate the (potentially customized) interface specifications and implementations (see [Note for IOService builder](#ioservice-builder-note))
* setup the internal message queues
* configure IOServer nodes - what services to run with which pattern setup on what datacontexts and nodes against which queues
* configure Camel routes using these queues and deploy them in the Integrator
* implement and setup automated functional and integration tests for the used interfaces

All (close to) synchronous request/response patterns are realized as SOAP XML services, the SOAP operation name is transferred as an application header.
Standard Soap fault messages are delivered (and expected) in all error cases that are not covered by the fault type declared in the service.
All one-way communications will be realized as plain XML messages, any required dispatching is implemented in the service handler.
There is a common fault type structure available for the standard interfaces, SOAP as well as plain XML.
This ServiceError structure allows to communicate the desired level of context information for the error including the failed message.
The ServiceError contains a copy of the source message that failed but only if the source message is not larger than 10 kB.

Each generated service has its own self-contained XML namespace, common structures are thus repeated in each namespace.
A side effect is that the “common structures” are effectively different types that just look the same.
This choice has been made to simplify the packaging and avoid problems when deploying different versions of different interfaces together.
We deemed it more important to avoid the complexity of trying to keep “almost common” structures apart and handling different versions of shared namespace types
than to tune for maximum reuse potential of code between applications or modules using different interfaces.
The interfaces are versioned in two ways, on the namespace level for braking changes (major version) and on the message level for minor changes.
The namespace name for each interface contains the major version of that interface,
so different major versions of the same interface will have different namespace names.
Each message carries a fixed value “version” property to indicate the (major.minor) version of the message structure. This version number is changed
whenever the structure chnages for the actual message, i.e. an interface can support messages of different (minor) message versions at the same time.
Additionally all messages carry a “created” timestamp and a “source” property indicating the logical source of the message - a system, module or flow.
Messages from different sources can be routed to the same queues and service instances.

For the XML style we have chosen an approach where primitive type values are represented as XML attributes
while longer text, structures and collections are represented as elements. This provides a comparably
compact structure that can be consumed by both tools and humans and emphasises the structural view
(by handling values and structures differently).
We do use standard XML data types where available; the documents should be UTF-8 encoded and date/time values are expected to always be in UTC.

###### 1.1.1. Note for IOService builder

In some IOService builder configuration examples, the protocol is given using two alternatives separated by a vertical bar, such as
`protocol="plainxml|soap"`. This is a documentation shortcut indicating that the configuration can be used with either of the two protocols.
In a real configuration, only one protocol can be specified at a time.

##### 1.2. Interface Patterns

The JCMS standard interfaces provide the opportunity to use different communication patterns and external protocols.
This section will provide the general assumptions and constraints as well as recommendations.
In many cases the same payload message formats can be used for different patterns as the JCMS system is
designed to deal with different communication patterns on a protocol level.
There are some restrictions though that will be mentioned in the sections describing the concrete format types.

The standard Interfaces are implemented as IOServer service handler; that means the actual business functionality is executed
in an IOServer worker process. The IOServer communicates with its clients through the JCMS internal message broker,
today a QPid broker (migration to ActiveMQ planned). Communication to external systems is handled by gateway/router applications,
preferably JEE based (Camel routes) or DIG channels where that is required for compatibility reasons.
The external communication protocol can be chosen from the wide range of Camel plugins.
Protocols with support for application headers are preferred as they can benefit from the JCMS IOServer Meta information
(e.g. state references).
The concrete requirements are given by the performance/throughput, reliability and security requirements of the installation.

###### 1.2.1. Data input from upstream systems

For information transfer to JCMS from upstream systems most often a publish/subscribe mechanism is suitable.
JCMS will handle the information when it becomes available or it might pull an external source
(e.g. ftp server) for information on configured occasions (periodic or scheduled).
Typically the sending system is expected to be master of the sent information (relative to JCMS)
and doesn’t need any feedback whether the message could be handled.

For more complex situations it is recommended to use a
service with ACK response and state references to handle in the air collisions and similar situations.
This applies especially for two way synchronizations or when JCMS is (partial) master.
Also it is a good solution for online services that have a potential high level of dependencies between messages
because of compound state replacement semantic, e.g. if the roster state input is used for online synchronization.

###### 1.2.2. Data output to downstream systems

For information transfer from JCMS to downstream systems a number of options are available, depending on the synchronization requirements.
In most cases the transfer is triggered from inside the JCMS system; scheduled, periodic or when certain events occur (e.g. on change),
it is also possible to transfer on request. JCMS standard interfaces are not prepared to initiate business actions based on
acknowledgement status received for JCMS initiated transfers, normally they will only be logged.

###### 1.2.3. Business service

Additional to plain data transfer the standard interfaces will also support business services
(e.g. crew check-in, legality checks or other calculations).

For more details regarding protocol and pattern choices refer to the “Data Gateway SAD” document (tbd).

##### 1.3. Interface in IOServer

###### 1.3.1. IOServer data context

IOServer loads a plan with a data context which has a given period.
For instance, the time window can be from “current planning month - 1” to “current planning month + 2”.
The validity period of the business rules are applied within this time window.
For some interfaces, it makes sense to verify that the data input/output
sent by request messages belongs to that time window.
As a result, a message is rejected with an error message
if it can not be dealt with in a reasonable way.

Below is a list standard interfaces which requests must be within loaded data context:

* Trip Input: request message must contain trips that have activities and and flight legs
  which are within data context.
* Trip Output: attributes **periodStart** and **periodEnd** in getTripsInPeriodRequest
  message must be within data context
* Crew Roster Input:
* Crew Roster Output: attributes **periodStart** and **periodEnd** message must be
  within data context
* Flight Schedule Input:request message must contain *scheduledLeg* that has **scheduledStartTime**
  and **scheduledEndTime** are within data context.
* Operational Flight Input: request message must contain time attributes within data context.
* Crew On Flight: attribute **dataOfOrigin** in request message must be within
  data context

##### 1.4. Naming Conventions

The standard interfaces naming style follows JAVA conventions, i.e. CamelCase for types, camelCase for element and attribute names.
Attribute (and simple type elemnt) names are chosen to express the business meaning of the represented property,
element names for complex types are the name of the logical object or a combination of operation verbs with the name.

It is recommended to follow the same conventions when customizing services.
Usage of client specific names for business objects and properties is of course expected,
but the naming style and usage of operation verbs should be consistent.

###### 1.4.1. Object and property names

Naming of objects and properties in the standard interfaces follows the JCMS established business wording. That means for example:
A trip is a grouping of activities for a given set of anonymous crew; the same thing is called pairing or crew rotation in some places.
A rotation is an anonymous aircraft rotation, a set of legs that are assigned to the same not yet known aircraft.

###### 1.4.2. semantic of xml element names

The xml messages’ complex type elements fall into three catgories:

object state element
:   contain the state of the represented object,
    simple properties are attributes or simple type elements directly on this level.
    All complex type children are *object state elements* .

    The element name is the name of the logical object, potentially prepended by a
    state verb like *add* or *replace*.

    An element without a verb prefix has the same semantics as *put*. For example in the trip\_state\_input
    service *addTrip*, *replaceTrip* and *trip* are used while in the flight
    interface there is *addFlight* and *putFlight*.

verb element
:   contain a group of properties of a logical object to be updated together,
    simple properties are attributes or simple type elements directly on this level.
    All complex type children are *object state element*.

    The element name is an operation verb like *update*.

object change element
:   contain (partial) changes for a logical object,
    only identifying properties are present on the top level.
    New values for simple type properties are captured in
    children of type *verb element*.
    Complex type children are *object state element*,
    *verb element*. or *object change element*.

    > The element name is the name of the logical object
    > prepended by an operation verb like *update* or *set*.

State verbs describe operations on full object state, like add or replace.
The element is an *object state element*.
The verb can be the name of a business operation if applicable.
The common state verbs have the following meaning:

add
:   Insert a new object with the given state.

    The operation will fail if the object already exists.

replace
:   Modify an existing object
    to reflect the new state. This can include the implicit deletion of
    child objects that are no longer part of the represented state.

    The operation will fail if the object doesn’t exists.

put
:   Create a new object or modify an existing object
    to reflect the new state (i.e. *add* or *replace*).
    This can include the implicit deletion of
    child objects that are no longer part of the represented state.

cancel
:   Logically delete the object, but keep information about its state.
    If the object is added again later the old information
    is used as defaults (reinstantiation).

    The element typically contains extended identification
    information only.

    The operation will fail if the object doesn’t exist.

delete
:   Delete the object and forget about it’s state.
    If the object is added again, no information is inherited.

    The element typically contains extended identification
    information only.

    The operation will not fail even if the object doesn’t exist.

Operation verbs can be the name of a business operation if applicable,
or they describe the type of change that is expected.
The element is an *object change element* or *verb element*.
The common operation verbs have the following meaning

update
:   Modify the logical object
    according to the information in the provided sub-elements.

    Children that are not mentioned in the element are not affected,
    but note that a subelement could be of *object state element*
    with *replace* semantic.

    The operation will fail if the object doesn’t exist.

set
:   Create the object if it doesn’t exist, or modify it
    according to information in the provided sub-elements.

    Children that are not mentioned in the element are not affected,
    but note that a subelement could be of *object state element*
    with *replace* semantic.

    The operation might fail if the object doesn’t exist and
    the element doesn’t contain all required data to create one.

terminate
:   Close the validity period of the object.

    The element typically contains (extended) identification
    information and the termination date or datetime.

    The operation will not fail even if the object doesn’t exist.

##### 1.5. Matching of Planning Objects

Trips are normally identified by a “name” (string) and a “dateOfOrigin” (date).
In the default implementation it is assumed that the pair (name, dateOfOrigin) is unique within
the loaded plan.
If name is not provided matching cannot be done, and duplicate objects might exist in the plan, as new
trips will get a generated name.
A custom implementation can map a customer’s specific id attribute to a custom field and/or use
other attribute combinations to identify trips.

Not all planning objects have stable business keys, for example generic activities are defined
entirely by their data.

All attributes that are included for the planning object are used to match the existing objects in JCMS.
Normally it is recommended to always provide all known values for available attributes,
but if some attributes should explicitly not be considered, don’t include them in the message.

Start and end times of objects are considered matches if they differ less than a configurable number of minutes.
This is called fuzzy time matching.
The closer the found value is, the better the match is considered.
Example: fuzzy matching are used for deviations in departure and arrival times and the “closest match” leg will be chosen if the IATA key is no longer unique (e.g. due to diversion back to base).

If several objects would provide a best match the operation will fail due to ambiguity.

Operations that explicitly require the object not to exist will fail if any object is found.

Operations that require existence will fail if no object is found.

Operations for which the resulting state in JCMS is the same regardless if the object is found or not, will not fail if no object is found.
This applies to “delete” and “terminate” operations.

##### 1.6. Reference data lookup

The standard interfaces generally expect that the attributes and elements that refer to other objects inside JCMS can only contain
existing values. Missing references are treated as message errors. The expectations about business object references
are normally spelled out per interface, but catalog data is typically always expected to exist.
If the documentation doesn’t explicitly mention that a reference will be created or ignored (i.e. not set), then
the default behavior is to fail if the referenced object doesn’t exist.

The default implementation of catalog lookup uses the primary key in JCMS, mapping of other keys can be implemented
in customization where needed, see below for more information on customization. Note that all references to catalog
data are case sensitive.

##### 1.7. Dates and Times

The handling of dates and timestamps is a common source of misunderstanding. In this section the basic concepts of dates
and times are explained in the context of Standard Interfaces, although it’s also generally valid for the JCMS system at large.

###### 1.7.1. Timestamps

Internally, JCMS represents timestamps or “a specific instant of time” with the type AbsTime. The AbsTime type has minute level
resolution i.e. JCMS never stores seconds or fraction of seconds when representing timestamps for any business domain object.
In interface schemas, the AbsTime type maps to the xs:dateTime type. In inbound interfaces, when mapping from xs:dateTime to
AbsTime, seconds and fractions are ignored. Generally, if not otherwise explicitly noted, timestamps sent to JCMS through Standard
Interfaces are always expected to be in UTC. An xs:dateTime without the letter “Z” (which identifies UTC) and without explicit
timezone offset is interpreted as UTC. If a timezone offset is provided, it is used for converting and storing the internal AbsTime
as UTC. See mapping examples below:

| xs:dateTime | AbsTime |
| --- | --- |
| 2016-10-26T21:32:52.12679 | 26OCT2016 21:32 |
| 2016-10-26T21:32:52 | 26OCT2016 21:32 |
| 2016-10-26T21:32:52Z | 26OCT2016 21:32 |
| 2016-10-26T21:32:52+00:00 | 26OCT2016 21:32 |
| 2016-10-26T21:32:52+02:00 | 26OCT2016 19:32 |
| 2016-10-26T21:32:52-07:00 | 27OCT2016 04:32 |

In outbound interfaces, when converting from AbsTime to xs:dateTime, the seconds part is always set to 00 and a letter “Z” is
appended to denote UTC:

| AbsTime | xs:dateTime |
| --- | --- |
| 26OCT2016 21:32 | 2016-10-26T21:32:00Z |

###### 1.7.2. Dates

Dates are represented internally in JCMS with the type AbsDate. Unless otherwise explicitly noted, a date is always timezone
neutral. In interface schemas, the AbsDate type maps to the xs:date type. Typical business objects in JCMS represented by
AbsDate are “date of birth” and various properties used for identifying an object, e.g. “date of origin” which is part of the
identifier for flight legs. In cases where a date is used to represent the validity of a business object, e.g. passport expiry
date, it may be necessary to define on a business level how to interpret at which “instance of time” the validity of the passport
actually ends. Since the AbsDate is timezone neutral, the end of validity could be interpreted as the end of the expiry date
regardless of timezone, or, it could be defined as the end of the expiry date in a certain timezone, e.g. UTC.

###### 1.7.3. Validity periods

In contrary to the example of passport validity above, business level validity is normally represented in JCMS using the
“validity period” pattern. A validity period is defined by two AbsTime timestamps *validFrom* and *validTo* such that an object is
valid at all instants of time t, where:

```
validFrom <= t < validTo
```

Important to notice is that the “instant of time” represented by validFrom is **included** in the validity period whereas validTo is **excluded**.
Also important to note is that validTo is optional. If left out it means that the object is valid “forever” or “until futher notice”.
Examples of objects for which the validity is defined this way are crew contracts, employments and qualifications.
Several validity periods can be stored in JCMS for the same object in what is logically referred to as a *timeline*. As an example,
when looking at the records for a certain crew member over time, there may be several periods, both past, current and perhaps even
future, during which a specific aircraft qualification was/is/will be valid. See example below:

![../_images/timeline.png](../_images/timeline.png)

In this example the timeline consists of 5 validity periods:

```
validFrom = 1JAN2010 08:00 (UTC); validTo = 1MAR2011 08:00 (UTC)
validFrom = 1JAN2012 08:00 (UTC); validTo = 1JAN2013 08:00 (UTC)
validFrom = 1JAN2013 08:00 (UTC); validTo = 1JAN2014 08:00 (UTC)
validFrom = 1JAN2014 08:00 (UTC); validTo = 1JAN2015 08:00 (UTC)
validFrom = 1SEP2015 08:00 (UTC); validTo = 1NOV2016 08:00 (UTC)
```

When stored in JCMS, validity periods for a certain object are never overlapping. Between *different* objects on the other hand there may
of course be overlaps, e.g. a crew member may have more than one airport qualification valid at the same time.
Notice from the example above that the object is valid consecutively throughout the period from 1JAN2012 08:00 until 1JAN2015 08:00 although
technically represented by 3 different validity periods. Given the definition of a validity period above, it is important to understand that
every discrete “instant of time” within this period is included in one and only one of these validity periods.

Assume for example that crew qualifications are imported into JCMS from an external HR system in which qualification records are stored with
an acquisition date and an expiration date:

```
Qualification records for Captain John Doe
B737; acquisition date = 2004-03-01; expiration date 2008-02-29
B747; acquisition date = 2009-05-01; expiration date 2010-04-30
B747; acquisition date = 2010-05-01; expiration date 2011-04-30
B747; acquisition date = 2011-05-01; expiration date 2012-04-30
```

Captain John Doe started his career in the B737 fleet but later switched to B747. Since first acquiring his B747 qualification it has been
renewed once a year as indicated by the records. The business interpretation of these dates is that John Doe has a consecutive qualification
for B747 from 2009-05-01 until (and including) 2012-04-30.

When importing this data into JCMS using the Standard Interfaces, these qualification acquisitions and expirations must be expressed as
JCMS validity periods, i.e. with validFrom and validTo timestamps in xs:dateTime format. In order to retain the same business
interpretation also in the JCMS model, care must be taken when converting acquisition and expiration dates into timestamps in order to
avoid gaps in the JCMS timeline. A correct representation, based on the definition of validity periods in JCMS, may look as follows:

```
B737; validFrom = 2004-03-01T00:00:00; validTo = 2008-03-01T00:00:00
B747; validFrom = 2009-05-01T00:00:00; validTo = 2010-05-01T00:00:00
B747; validFrom = 2010-05-01T00:00:00; validTo = 2011-05-01T00:00:00
B747; validFrom = 2011-05-01T00:00:00; validTo = 2012-05-01T00:00:00
```

Note that when mapped to AbsTime, these timestamps are interpreted as UTC. If it’s more correct from a business point of view to express
the validity in a specific timezone, an offset may be added. If e.g. the HR system of an airline on the American west coast stores
qualifications acquired at local bases, it would probably be more correct to express the validity of these qualifications in local times:

```
B737; validFrom = 2004-03-01T00:00:00-08:00; validTo = 2008-03-01T00:00:00-08:00
B747; validFrom = 2009-05-01T00:00:00-08:00; validTo = 2010-05-01T00:00:00-08:00
B747; validFrom = 2010-05-01T00:00:00-08:00; validTo = 2011-05-01T00:00:00-08:00
B747; validFrom = 2011-05-01T00:00:00-08:00; validTo = 2012-05-01T00:00:00-08:00
```

##### 1.8. Customization points

The standard interfaces are built using SMOG which allows very flexible customization.
The interface structures can easily be modified using the SMOG syntax (for details see the SMOG documentation).

The standard interfaces’ more complex logic, especially lookup, checking and business operations are implemented in Python helper modules
delivered with the system. Each module has classes that represent the logic on a certain level of the interface operation.

To customize the behaviour of the standard Python helper modules, you create custom modules that inherit from the classes in the core module and
override or add to the standard behaviour.
This is the easiest way to achieve customized matching of business objects or to
automatically create custom extension objects together with the parent business object.

To use the customized module you need to make changes in the SMOG service mapping. The *import* element on the request level must be customized to load the custom module instead.

In some cases the standard interfaces rely on Rave variables to define the behavior of the interface. These
Rave variables are defined in a CARMSYS Rave module called ‘interfaces\_core’. However this module is just
an empty “stub” interface. The actual implementation of these Rave variables need to be done as a part of
a customer delivery. Typically the customer CARMUSR will have a Rave module e.g. ‘interfaces’ that
inherits from ‘interfaces\_core’ and redefines the Rave variables.

### Interface Implementation Patterns


The JCMS standard interfaces support a couple of implementation patterns to ease
configuration. This chapter describes some of these that might require a bit more context.

##### 2.1. Message Receivers

The **Message Receivers** pattern provides a way to deliver the same logical stream of information
in a variety of formats to different downstream systems. This pattern can in principle
be applied to any interface that produces outbound messages but it is most useful
for interfaces that are triggered from within JCMS.

###### 2.1.1. Concept

This pattern allows the registration of one or more receivers to an outbound interface.
A *receiver* should be seen as a “logical receiver”, and is not necessarily the same
as an external system receiving the messages since there might be several
external systems receiving same stream of messages for one and the same *receiver*.

A *logical receiver* is represented by a `MessageFormatter` plugin that is registered
for a sink to an interface which is prepared for it with a `MessageGenerator`.
The mapping will invoke the generator’s `format` function as a post-processing step,
which in turn will call the format functions of all registered formatters
and send all produced messages to the corresponding sinks.
A formatter can produce a list of 0-n messages for each
output produced by the underlying interface and also modify the headers, so it can
change encoding or soap method, use different content types and also implement
message splitting or filter the data as needed.

###### 2.1.2. Implementation

JCMS standard interfaces support for receivers is implemented in the python module
`jcms.std_interfaces.common`. The module provides a base classes `MessageGenerator`
and `MessageFormatter`, as well as an implementation of `NativeProtocolFormatter`
which does format the output in the underlying services native format.

To utilize receivers, an interface has to create a MessageGenerator instance
and register the wanted formatters with apropriate queue names. The
`MessageGenerator.format` classmethod (or an overloaded version) must be invoked
as postprocessor for the correct operation. It will use the latest generator
instance automatically as its captured in a class level instance.
The following snippet shows an example of a client mapping using two receivers.

```
<service-mapping xmlns="http://namespace.jeppesen.com/smog/v2" target="air2_mave2" language="Python">
<include href="../std_interfaces.common/base_4_mapping.xml"/>

<client-impl service_name="MyService" service_version="1">
    <runtime-parameters>
    <!-- all required parameters -->
    </runtime-parameters>
    <post-process name="format" operation="outputOperation" process_struct="true"
                module="std_interfaces.common" function="MessageGenerator.format"/>
</client-impl>

<output-mapping struct="my_module.MyUpdateMsg">
    <import alias="common" name="std_interfaces.common"/>
    <import alias="formatters" name="my_special_formatters"/>
    <assign name="generator" expr="common.MessageGenerator()"/>
    <call name="add_receiver_native" expr="generator.add_receiver('from.ioservice.MyService', common.NativeProtocolFormatter())"/>
    <call name="add_receiver_custom" expr="generator.add_receiver('from.ioservice.MyService.extra', formatters.MyFormatter())"/>
    <!-- additional logic as needed -->
</output-mapping>
</service-mapping>
```

Note especially the parameter `process_struct="true"` in the post-process definition,
which will advise the service to pass the unformatted SmogStruct instance to the
MessageGenerator.format function. That allows each formatter to apply its own format
to the struct directly instead of parsing the native format first.

For each new receiver, a subclass of `MessageFormatter` must be implemented,
especially providing the `format(payload,headers)` method.
The payload is the SmogStruct (or formatted message depending on the `process_struct` parameter)
of the message produced by the underlying service, which is a request in case of a client
and response in case of a server implementation. The method shall return two
lists `[messages],[headers]` the first being the list of all messages to emit (can be empty)
and the second the list of the corresponding header-dictionaries.
Note that each list entry MUST be a separate dict instance,
do not include the same dict several times. The MessageFormatter base class method
`get_msg_headers` can be used to obtain the required copies.
It is strongly recommended to overload that method to handle
updates to the header dict (e.g. setting content type or encoding).

###### 2.1.3. Examples

To see examples of receiver usage in the standard interfaces, please have a look
at the following interfaces:

* Flight Events see [Flight Events](flight_events.html#stdif-flight-events)
* Flight Chat see stdif-flight-chat-out

##### 2.2. Subscription Management

**Subscription Management** is the capability of a system to keep track of subscription
configuration for downstream systems and publish a consistent stream of messages
that match the configuration. It is typically expected that this configuration can
be updated at runtime without restart of the affected interface(s).
Subscription Management applies only to interfaces that are triggered from within JCMS.
The JCMS standard interfaces utilize the support for basic subscription management
provided by ioservice\_builder.
With this feature it is not possible to dynamically add or remove subscriptions at runtime,
but the configuration of statically registered subscriptions can be
changed at runtime if that is enabled for the interface in question.

###### 2.2.1. Concept

A managed subscription configures a *Filter* for the data that shall be exported.
The *Trigger* will evaluate the runtime configuration to determine the active Filter,
and decide what changes and/or load messages to send.

There are three main types of subscriptions supported by JCMS.

A **request based subscription** will only send data after a filter has been explicitly requested.
After the request has been received, the interface will send a full load of the filtered dataset,
followed by change messages for updates for the provided data.
The filter is kept until a new request is received, and a new load is only sent
when the filter actually changes.

A **gliding subscripton** maintains a filter that is defined relative to
a given point in time. The filter is constructed on every invocation based on NOW
and all matching change messages are sent out. There is no load.

A **moving subscription** also bases its filter definition on a point in time.
But the filter will only be set at certain occasions, relative to a *due time*.
When the filter changes, a full load of the filtered dataset is sent,
followed by change messages for updates for the provided data.
The filter is kept until the next update occasion.

To maintain the order between all messages, including state load and updates, and
to make sure no updates are missed, a subscription trigger runs two operations on each invocation,
first the **delta phase** and then the **load phase**.
During the delta phase, gliding subscriptions will create the new filter, while
other subscriptions keep the currently active filter (if there is any). All
pending updates for that filter will be sent out to make sure the current scope is up to date.
At start of the load phase, the trigger will check whether there is any pending
configuration request and execute it if that’s the case. Then it will check
whether a new filter needs to be created (except for gliding subscriptions),
and if the new filter differs from the previous a full load will be sent.
Each phase has its own interface mappings
and could be based on different services altogether if needed.

It is recommended to combine the *Subscription Management* pattern with the
*Message Receivers* pattern, see [Message Receivers](#stdif-receivers-pattern) to implement distinct
outbound feeds for different downstream systems based on the existing standard interfaces.

Support for *Subscription Management* is provided by a set of supporting classes,
including a base call for trigger implementations. Runtime updates of subscription
configuration, including filter requests for request based subscriptions,
can be made through the **Subscription Configuration** interface,
see [Subscription Configuration](#stdif-subscription-config).

###### 2.2.2. Implementation

The framework for subscription management is implemented in the python modules
`jcms.ioservice_builder.subscription`,
`jcms.ioservice_builder.filter` and `jcms.ioservice_builder.schedule`.
The `subscription.TriggerBase` class encapsulates the basic behavior of a trigger
with this capabilities. It can be subclassed to provide the specific interface implementation,
for details see the **ioservice builder** documentation.
The actual subscription is managed by the `subscription.Manager` class, in combination with
the `schedule.Schedule` and `filter.Filter` classes.

The `Manager` class is responsible for the configuration and the subscription control flow
inside the interface. It provides the methods `prepare_delta_phase` and `prepare_load_phase`
which are used by the `TriggerBase` handler to calculate the filter that should be used based on the configuration. It uses the
`ioservice_builder.kvstore` to save configuration and active filter when needed so that the state isn’t lost between runs.
The class also provides a couple `request_xxx` methods that allow the ingestion of a new schedule and/or filter.
These methods are utilized by the *Subscription Configuration* interface
(see [Subscription Configuration](#stdif-subscription-config)) to enable
runtime updates to interface subscriptions.

A mapping for managed subscription services can access the subscription manager instance
as `service_context.subscription_manager` and should pass on the Filter instance
`service_context.subscription_manager.filter` to the business logic that collects
the data for output. Filter instances provide the methods
`accept(...)` to check for matches and `ldapQuery(*names)` to build Mave query expressions for filtering data.
It is recommended to check `filter.is_empty` early to avoid costly evaluations that will be discarded anyway.

When using a PeriodFilter in **diff\_mode**, the `ldapQuery()` method returns a query expression based on the difference
between the current and previous filter periods in order to support the use case of generating a unique set of objects at
each full load occasion. The `accept(...)` method on the other hand is not affected by **diff\_mode**. However, for both
methods the **diff\_mode** behavior can be overridden through a parameter, e.g. `accept(..., diff_mode=True)`.

When using subscription management, it is possible to generate the full trigger module based on `TriggerBase` as described
in the **ioservice builder** documentation. It is also possible to use a *handler\_module* to encapsulate the
default logic. For an example, have a look at **jcms.std\_interfaces.crew\_on\_flight\_4.trigger**
or **jcms.std\_interfaces.flightchat.flight\_trigger** and the corresponding service mapping files.

###### 2.2.3. Subscription Configuration

A subscription configuration consists of a Filter and potentially a schedule.
The `Filter` encapsulates the condition that data for the subscription shall match
and the `Schedule` encapsulates the automated filter update described in the
concepts above. The configurable instances are represented in the stored configuration
by a factory name and factory parameters. For *Schedule* the factory name is
stored in the key *schedule* and the parameters in *params*, for *Filter* the
factory is stored as *filter* and the parameters as *select*.

Each subscription can have an **active** configuration and potentially a pending
**request** with new configuration, the *Subscription Configuration* interface
(see [Subscription Configuration](#stdif-subscription-config)) supports retrieving the configuration of
managed subscriptions, setting the **request** configuration and also clearing
the existing configuration to force a fresh load or re-apply the default setup.

To initialize a default subscription configuration, it is possible to update the
configuration dictionary directly or to instantiate the wanted schedule and filter class
and invoke the *manager.request(now\_time, schedule,filter)* method.
In the latter case the configuration will be activated in the load phase.
When providing configuration as a dictionary, AbsTime and RelTime parameters
can be provided in any format accepted by the *abstime* and *reltime* functions.

The following filter classes are provided by the `jcms.ioservice_builder.filter` module:

* **Filter**: the base class represents an empty filter that blocks all data, configured by

  ```
  { "filter" : "empty" }
  ```
* **AllFilter**: this is a convenience class to express a filter that accepts all data, configured by

  ```
  { "filter" : "all" }
  ```
* **PeriodFilter**: The data is filtered for a specific period, accepting AbsTime values
  that fall within or overlap the selection period,
  AbsTime *period\_start* included, AbsTime *period\_end* excluded.
  The filter period can be empty (if both boundaries are None),
  finite (if both boundaries are set), or open (when only one boundary is set).
  A PeriodFilter is configured like this:

  ```
  { "filter" : "period",
    "select" : { "period_start": "24MAR2014 00:00", "period_end": "26MAR2014 00:00"} }
  ```

  A PeriodFilter can be configured to operate in **diff\_mode** in which case the effective period is calculated
  as the part of the current filter period that is not overlapping with the period of the last full load.
  This means a **moving subscription** can be configured to only generate full load for objects that have not been
  previously included.
  Below the configuration for a PeriodFilter operating in **diff\_mode** is shown:

  ```
  { "filter" : "period",
    "select" : { diff_mode": "true", "period_start": "24MAR2014 00:00", "period_end": "26MAR2014 00:00"} }
  ```

  Once the filter has been updated, the previous values are also recorded:

  ```
  { "filter" : "period",
    "select" : { diff_mode": "true", "period_start": "25MAR2014 00:00", "period_end": "27MAR2014 00:00",
                                     "prev_period_start": "24MAR2014 00:00", "prev_period_end": "25MAR2014 00:00"} }
  ```

The following schedule classes are provided by the `jcms.ioservice_builder.schedule` module:

* **Schedule**: the base class represents a null-schedule that doesn’t handle any filter updates.
  It should not needed to be used explicitly, but can be configured as

  ```
  { "schedule" : "null" }
  ```
* **BasicGlidingSchedule**: This class provides a gliding update of the *period\_start* and *period\_end*
  filter parameters for a PeriodFilter or derived class. The *before* and *after* RelTime parameters
  define the width of the time window, the *floor* enum parameter defines the baseline.
  It can take the values “*day*”,”*week*”,”*month*” meaning before and after are calculated
  based on *now.xxx\_floor()* with xxx=floor instead of *now* which is used when *floor* is None.
  A gliding subscription can be configured like this:

  ```
  { "schedule" : "gliding", "filter" : "period",
    "params" : {"before": "00:00", "after": "24:00", "floor": "day"}
  }
  ```
* **BasicMovingSchedule**: This class supports the same filter update as *BasicGlidingSchedule*,
  but the filter is updated at distinct occasions defined by the additional parameters
  *time\_of\_day* , *day\_of\_week* and *week\_of\_month* or *day\_of\_month* which are lists of RelTime and int.
  The *day\_of\_week* is zero-based while *week\_of\_month* and *day\_of\_month* are 1-based. The latter ones also
  accept -1 meaning last week of month and last day of month respectively.
  The filter is set based on the *due time* (see below) instead of *now* to provide predictable boundaries.
  If *floor* is specified, the filter is based on *due time*.xxx\_floor().
  If *week\_of\_month* or *day\_of\_month* are provided, then the schedule is monthly.
  Otherwise its weekly (if *day\_of\_week* is provided) or daily.
  The *due time* is the most recent occasion based on the specified parameters, according to the following logic:

  + `now.month_floor() + nearest_weekday(day_of_month,day_of_week) + time_of_day`
  + `now.month_floor() + week_of_month + day_of_week + time_of_day`
  + `now.week_floor() + day_of_week + time_of_day`
  + `now.day_floor() + time_of_day`

  Note that specifying multiple update occasions combined with *floor* may have the effect that the filter
  period remains unchanged over several update occasions (as in the “weekly moving subscription” example below).
  In such situations the full load is still produced on all the configured update occasions.

  To instantiate some typical moving schedules, the class provides the convenience methods
  *daily*, *weekly* and *monthly* and *monthly\_weekday*. For details see the inline documentation.

  A daily moving subscription can be configured like this:

  ```
  { "schedule" : "moving", "filter" : "period",
    "params" : { "before": "00:00", "after": "24:00", "floor": "day",
                "time_of_day": "4:00" }
  }
  ```

  To run a load multiple times per day, each time moving the filter period based on the new time\_of\_day, use something like this:

  ```
  { "schedule" : "moving", "filter" : "period",
    "params" : { "before": "04:00", "after": "10:00",
                 "time_of_day": "4:00,16:00" }
  }
  ```

  A weekly moving subscription can be configured like this:

  ```
  { "schedule" : "moving", "filter" : "period",
    "params" : { "before": "1,00:00", "after": "3,00:00", "floor": "week",
                 "time_of_day": "4:00", "day_of_week" : "0,2,6" }
  }
  ```

  A monthly moving subscription running on specific dates looks like this:

  ```
  { "schedule" : "moving", "filter" : "period",
    "params" : { "before": "30,00:00", "after": "60,00:00", "floor": "month",
                 "time_of_day": "4:00", "day_of_month" : "1,12,-5" }
  }
  ```

  To run only on a specific weekday nearest to the date, use something like this:

  ```
  { "schedule" : "moving", "filter" : "period",
    "params" : { "before": "30,00:00", "after": "60,00:00", "floor": "month",
                 "time_of_day": "4:00",
                 "day_of_month" : "1,15", "day_of_week" : "0" }
  }
  ```

  To run on first and last Saturday each month would look like this:

  ```
  { "schedule" : "moving", "filter" : "period",
    "params" : { "before": "30,00:00", "after": "60,00:00", "floor": "month",
                 "time_of_day": "4:00",
                 "week_of_month" : "1,-1", "day_of_week" : "5" }
  }
  ```

####### 2.2.3.1. Sample ioservice\_builder configuration

```
<ioservice name="flight_opswindow" pattern="repeatingtrigger" >
    <description>A trigger sending flight data twice a day in diff_mode for a daily moving operational window.</description>
    <subscription>
      <moving name="moving" before="0:00" after="48:00" floor="day" time_of_day="0:30, 5:00"/>
      <filter name="period" diff_mode="true" />
    </subscription>
    <delta-service name="MyFlightService1" version="1.0" protocol="soap"
       method="make_updateFlights_request">
        <service-spec location="$CARMUSR/data/config/smog/flight/service.xml"/>
        <protocol-spec location="$CARMUSR/data/config/smog/flight/protocol.xml"/>
        <service-mapping location="$CARMUSR/data/config/smog/flight/delta_mapping.xml"/>
        <parameter name="source" value="Me"/>
    </delta-service>
    <load-service name="MyFlightService1" version="1.0" protocol="soap"
       method="make_updateFlights_request">
        <service-spec location="$CARMUSR/data/config/smog/flight/service.xml"/>
        <protocol-spec location="$CARMUSR/data/config/smog/flight/protocol.xml"/>
        <service-mapping location="$CARMUSR/data/config/smog/flight/load_mapping.xml"/>
        <parameter name="source" value="Me"/>
    </load-service>
</ioservice>
```

### Aircraft Data Input


This chapter describes the interfaces that can be used to provide aircraft data to JCMS.

In JCMS aircraft data is valid during certain time periods. For parts of the information the validity is
actually an important part of the business data, for example it is important to know if and when an aircraft may change type or
seat configuration due to modifications, for example by adding winglets that transform a type from 752 to 75W.

Aircraft information is sometimes provided by systems that do not have validity information, and only knows the current state of each aircraft.
In this case a message implicitly has the semantics “this is what is valid now” where now is the time when the message was sent.
For such systems, without validity information, JCMS offers a “plain mode” of transferring the data (by using the `setAircraftDataPlain` operation),
where information always is interpreted as “valid now”. If the values in “plain mode” message differ from the currently valid
values in JCMS, a new validity record is created starting at the message creation time, ranging until further notice - or until any
future change of the same attribute(s)that is already registered in the system. The creation time of the message must be specified in UTC.

If the source system has validity information, then it should send the information using (“validity mode”) and message has
the semantics: “this is true for the given period of time”, where the start of the period is required and
the end could be left out (which means “until infinity”). In difference from the plain mode new values in such a
message will override any future values already present in the JCMS system if they overlap with the stated validity
from the message. The “validFrom” and “validTo” values must be specified in UTC.

Aircrafts are always identified by its `registration` number which is assumed to be the same between all talking
systems and constant over the lifetime of an aircraft data entry. In general the sending system is regarded master for the provided information.
Applications in JCMS require aircrafts to have a type, 752, 75W, etc. It is important that systems using this interface provide the correct `aircraftType` information.

Latest version of this interface is 2.

[Link to AircraftDataInput\_2.xsd](contract/std_interfaces.aircraft_input_2/AircraftDataInput_2.xsd)

[Link to AircraftDataInput\_2.wsdl](contract/std_interfaces.aircraft_input_2/AircraftDataInput_2.xsd)

Previous versions of this interface

[Link to AircraftDataPlain\_1\_2.xsd](contract/std_interfaces.aircraft_input_1_2/AircraftDataPlain_1_2.xsd)

[Link to AircraftDataValidity\_1\_2.xsd](contract/std_interfaces.aircraft_input_1_2/AircraftDataValidity_1_2.xsd)

Available operations are:

* ping
  :   Pings the service without doing anything (for test purposes).
* setAircraftDataPlain
  :   Set currently valid information for aircrafts (one-way request without any response message).
* setAircraftDataPlainWithAck
  :   Same as setAircraftDataPlain but with an acknowledge response on successful update (request/response).
* setAircraftDataValidity
  :   Set historic, current or future information for aircrafts (one-way request without any response message).
* setAircraftDataValidityWithAck
  :   Same as setAircraftDataValidity but with an acknowledge response on successful update (request/response).

##### 3.1. Life cycle of aircrafts

Aircraft that are out of service or retired must no longer be visible to planning applications in JCMS.
JCMS defines an aircraft as not available by “terminating” the validity of the aircraft’s type. It is worth pointing out
however that the Aircraft Data Input interface itself does not have a notion about whether an aircraft is “terminated” or not.
This means, any aircraft in the JCMS can be updated through the interface, also if they are no longer
valid from a business perspective.

##### 3.2. Interface capabilities (plain)

The `setAircraftDataPlain` operations are used for communicating aircraft information interpreted as “valid now” to JCMS, i.e. all information
in the message is currently valid in the sending system. This operation is useful for systems that knows the currently
valid information but doesn’t keep track of historical and future aircraft information. Internally JCMS stores most aircraft
information with time validity. Information received over `setAircraftDataPlain` operations is valid from the `created` time given
in the message and until next existing record in JCMS starts. If no such record exists in JCMS, the given value is valid
until further notice.

Information **is not** updated as a state, i.e. the service operates only on aircraft data entries in JCMS identified by their `registration` number as specified in incoming request.
Aircraft data entries existing in JCMS, but not in the incoming request, are not modified or removed from JCMS.

##### 3.3. Interface capabilities (validity)

The `setAircraftDataValidity` operations are used for communicating aircraft information with time validity to JCMS, i.e. all information
in the message is valid for certain time periods. This service is useful for systems that keep track of
historical and future aircraft information.

Information **is not** updated as a state, i.e. the service operates only on aircraft data entries in JCMS identified by their `registration` number as specified in incoming request.
Aircraft data entries existing in JCMS, but not in the incoming request, are not modified or removed from JCMS.

##### 3.4. Seat configuration

Seat configurations (number of seats per available seat class) can be predefined in JCMS and named with a short identifier,
for example 737-A3.
Aircraft seat configurations can be provided to the interface using the `seatConfiguration` field.
The provided value can refer to the short identifier of a predefined seat configuration, for example 737-A3.

Instead of referring to a predefined seat configuration, the value can declare the number of seats for different
seat classes using a specific format, for example F32I24P20. Each character (one or two chars) represents the seat class and the following
number represents the number of seats for that class.

##### 3.5. Detailed use cases (plain)

###### 3.5.1. Create/update aircraft information

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<setAircraftDataPlainRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="aircraft system" created="2015-01-01T00:00:00Z">
    <setAircraft registration="A123BC" noseNumber="A12B" serialNumber="0123456">
        <detail aircraftType="752" owner="AA" seatConfiguration="F32I24P20"/>
    </setAircraft>
</setAircraftDataPlainRequest>
```

The message above creates or updates aircraft “A123BC” in JCMS.
The optional nose- and serial number properties of the aircraft are set to the values provided in the message.
The type (752) and airline owner (AA) of the aircraft is valid from the created time (in UTC) of the message until further notice.

*State of aircraft in JCMS*

| regno | noseno | serialno | validfrom | validto | actype | owner | seat configuration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20150101 00:00 | null | 752 | AA | F32I24P20 |

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<setAircraftDataPlainRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="aircraft system" created="2015-01-02T00:00:00Z">
    <setAircraft registration="A123BC" noseNumber="A12B" serialNumber="0123456">
        <detail aircraftType="752" owner="AA" seatConfiguration="F32I24P20"/>
    </setAircraft>
</setAircraftDataPlainRequest>
```

The message above contains same information as was previously sent for aircraft “A123BC”, but creation time is one day later.
This is the typical case when information is exported from source system to JCMS each day, but the aircraft has not been updated in the source system.

The provided values doesn’t differ from the currently valid values in JCMS, no update is needed in JCMS.

*State of aircraft in JCMS*

| regno | noseno | serialno | validfrom | validto | actype | owner | seat configuration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20150101 00:00 | null | 752 | AA | F32I24P20 |

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<setAircraftDataPlainRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="aircraft system" created="2015-02-01T00:00:00Z">
    <setAircraft registration="A123BC" noseNumber="A12B" serialNumber="0123456">
        <detail aircraftType="75W" owner="AA" seatConfiguration="F20I40P20"/>
    </setAircraft>
</setAircraftDataPlainRequest>
```

The message above contains an updated the type for aircraft “A123BC”, and creation time is one month later.
The current type in JCMS (752) is replaced with the new type (75W) at the created time of the message ranging until further notice.
The seat configuration has also been updated.

*State of aircraft in JCMS*

| regno | noseno | serialno | validfrom | validto | actype | owner | seat configuration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20150101 00:00 | 20150201 00:00 | 752 | AA | F32I24P20 |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20150201 00:00 | null | 75W | AA | F20I40P20 |

###### 3.5.2. Terminate aircraft information (plain)

It’s possible for external systems to communicate that an aircraft is no longer available using AircraftDataPlain service.
This is done by specifying the aircraftType to an empty value in the request message.

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<setAircraftDataPlainRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="aircraft system" created="2015-03-01T00:00:00Z">
    <setAircraft registration="A123BC" noseNumber="A12B" serialNumber="0123456">
        <detail aircraftType=""/>
    </setAircraft>
</setAircraftDataPlainRequest>
```

The message above specifies an empty value as the type for aircraft “A123BC”, and creation time is one month later.
The aircraft validity is closed at the created time of the message.

*State of aircraft in JCMS*

| regno | noseno | serialno | validfrom | validto | actype | owner | seat configuration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20150101 00:00 | 20150201 00:00 | 752 | AA | F32I24P20 |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20150201 00:00 | 20150301 00:00 | 75W | AA | F20I40P20 |

The aircraft “A123BC” is no longer available after 20150301 00:00.

##### 3.6. Detailed use cases (validity)

###### 3.6.1. Create/update aircraft information

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<setAircraftDataValidityRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="aircraft_system" created="2014-11-30T12:21:00Z">
    <setAircraft registration="A123BC" noseNumber="A12B" serialNumber="0123456">
        <detail aircraftType="752" owner="AA" validFrom="2012-01-01T00:00:00Z" validTo="2014-03-01T00:00:00Z"/>
        <detail aircraftType="75M" owner="AA" validFrom="2014-07-15T00:00:00Z"/>
    </setAircraft>
</setAircraftDataValidityRequest>
```

The message above creates or updates aircraft with key “A123BC” in JCMS.
The optional nose- and serial number properties of the aircraft are set to the values provided in the message.
The type and airline owner of the aircraft is set for the time periods (in UTC) provided in the message.

*State of aircraft in JCMS*

| regno | noseno | serialno | validfrom | validto | actype | owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20120101 00:00 | 20140301 00:00 | 752 | AA |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20140715 00:00 | null | 75M | AA |

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<setAircraftDataValidityRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="aircraft_system" created="2014-12-15T15:05:31Z">
    <setAircraft registration="A123BC" noseNumber="A12B" serialNumber="0123456">
        <detail aircraftType="75W" owner="AA" validFrom="2015-02-01T00:00:00Z" validTo="2015-06-01T00:00:00Z"/>
    </setAircraft>
</setAircraftDataValidityRequest>
```

The message above contains information for aircraft “A123BC”, but for another time period.
The type and airline owner of the aircraft is set for the time periods provided in the message.
Please note that the aircraft details **are not** updated as a state, i.e. other information, not overlapping
the time periods provided in the message, are not updated or removed in JCMS.

*State of aircraft in JCMS*

| regno | noseno | serialno | validfrom | validto | actype | owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20120101 00:00 | 20140301 00:00 | 752 | AA |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20140715 00:00 | 20150201 00:00 | 75M | AA |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20150201 00:00 | 20150601 00:00 | 75W | AA |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20150601 00:00 | null | 75M | AA |

###### 3.6.2. Terminate aircraft information (validity)

Aircrafts are terminated by providing the end date of the aircraft in the `clearDetails` element.

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<setAircraftDataValidityRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="aircraft_system" created="2014-12-15T15:05:31Z">
    <setAircraft registration="A123BC" noseNumber="A12B" serialNumber="0123456">
        <clearDetails removeFrom="2015-01-15T00:00:00Z"/>
    </setAircraft>
</setAircraftDataValidityRequest>
```

The message above contains information for aircraft “A123BC”, end date of the aircraft is provided in the terminateDetail element.

*State of aircraft in JCMS*

| regno | noseno | serialno | validfrom | validto | actype | owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20120101 00:00 | 20140301 00:00 | 752 | AA |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20140715 00:00 | 20150115 00:00 | 75M | AA |

The aircraft A123BC is no longer available after 20150115 00:00.

###### 3.6.3. Update aircraft information as a state

In order to communicate the full state of an aircraft, the `detail` elements must be combined with a `clearDetails` element.

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<setAircraftDataValidityRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="aircraft_system" created="2014-12-15T15:05:31Z">
    <setAircraft registration="A123BC" noseNumber="A12B" serialNumber="0123456">
      <clearDetails/>
      <detail aircraftType="752" owner="AA" seatConfiguration="F32I24P20" validFrom="2012-01-01T00:00:00Z" validTo="2013-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
      <detail aircraftType="75W" owner="AA" seatConfiguration="F32I24P20" validFrom="2013-02-15T00:00:00Z" validTo="2014-07-01T00:00:00Z"/>
      <detail aircraftType="75F" owner="AA" seatConfiguration="F20I40P20" validFrom="2014-07-15T00:00:00Z"/>  
    </setAircraft>
</setAircraftDataValidityRequest>
```

The message above contains the complete state of all periods for the aircraft “A123BC” combined with an instruction to clear any existing details.

*State of aircraft in JCMS*

| regno | noseno | serialno | validfrom | validto | actype | owner | seat configuration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20120101 00:00 | 20130101 00:00 | 752 | AA | F32I24P20 |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20130215 00:00 | 20140701 00:00 | 75W | AA | F32I24P20 |
| A123BC | A12B | 0123456 | 20140715 00:00 | null | 75F | AA | F20I40P20 |

##### 3.7. Providing invalid enumeration values in request message

The values “aircraftType” and “owner” in the incoming request message refer to catalog data defined in in JCMS.
Valid enumeration values for these types varies between installations and must be defined by each customer installation.
The complete message is rejected in case of providing enumeration values which doesn’t match the catalog data in JCMS.

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<setAircraftDataValidityRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="aircraft_system" created="2014-11-30T12:21:00Z">
    <setAircraft registration="A123BC" noseNumber="A12B" serialNumber="0123456">
        <detail aircraftType="752" owner="AA" validFrom="2012-01-01T00:00:00Z" validTo="2014-03-01T00:00:00Z"/>
        <detail aircraftType="777" owner="AA" validFrom="2014-07-15T00:00:00Z"/>
    </setAircraft>
</setAircraftDataValidityRequest>
```

The message above provides invalid enumeration value ‘777’ for “aircraftType”. The message is rejected and no changes are saved.
An error message with the following content is created by the interface and put on a static error queue.

```
<?xml version='1.0' encoding='UTF-8'?>
<setAircraftDataValidityFault xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="AircraftDataInput" code="MessageError" subcode="ReferenceNotFound" requestId="1">
  <reason>AircraftDetail.aircraftType, could not find any AircraftType with key '('777',)'</reason>
  <sourceMessage><![CDATA[<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<setAircraftDataValidityRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AircraftDataInput/v2" version="2" source="aircraft_system" created="2014-11-30T12:21:00Z">
    <setAircraft registration="A123BC" noseNumber="A12B" serialNumber="0123456">
        <detail aircraftType="752" owner="AA" validFrom="2012-01-01T00:00:00Z" validTo="2014-03-01T00:00:00Z"/>
        <detail aircraftType="777" owner="AA" validFrom="2014-07-15T00:00:00Z"/>
    </setAircraft>
</setAircraftDataValidityRequest>]]></sourceMessage>
</setAircraftDataValidityFault>
```

The error message states the reason for rejecting the message. In this case the provided value ‘777’ for “aircraftType”
is not found in the catalog data table aircraft\_type.
