### Airport Data Input


This chapter describes the interface that can be used to provide airport and related data to JCMS. Jeppesen provides
an up-to-date feed of airport master data that is made available to airline customers in a format that can
be imported by this interface.

The interface feed comprises airports and other related base data entities (countries, regions, country
subdivisions, cities, time zones and daylight saving time patterns).
The information represents a state per object, including time validity, for the objects included in the feed.
Objects that exist in the JCMS model but are not included in the feed are not affected. Objects that that
don’t exist in the model are created by the interface, initializing their complete history where applicable.
This applies to objects of any type, except airports marked as closed in the feed
(see [Handling of closed airports](#stdif-airport-input-closed-airports) below).
Objects that exist both in the model and in the feed are only updated if the data in the feed differ from
what is stored in the model. Only the parts of the data that differ are updated - this also applies to
historic data, i.e. the interface only updates the periods that actually differ. In order to limit the amount
of obsolete historic information transferred over the interface, the sending system may choose to exclude
historic information older than a certain date.

The current version of this interface is 2.

[Link to AirportDataValidity\_2.xsd](contract/std_interfaces.airport_input_2/AirportDataValidity_2.xsd)

The previous version of this interface is 1.0.

[Link to AirportDataValidity\_1\_0.xsd](contract/std_interfaces.airport_input_1_0/AirportDataValidity_1_0.xsd)

Note that version 2 is backward compatible with version 1.0 as a pre process step exists that transforms to the
:   difference namespace.

Available operations are:

* ping
  :   Pings the service without doing anything (for test purposes).
* setAirportDataValidity
  :   Allows to import information on one or more airports and other related base data entities to the JCMS database.
      (one-way request without any response message)
* setAirportDataValidityWithAck
  :   Allows to import information on one or more airports and other related base data entities to the JCMS database.
      (request/response)

##### 4.1. Supported airport key schemes

The key scheme controls what codes are used as key for airports in the JCMS model. Once an airport record has
been created in the model, the key is never changed.
The interface can be configured to use any of the predefined key schemes below. It is not allowed to change
key scheme in an existing installation, after an initial set of standard Jeppesen airport data has been imported.
The default airport key scheme is IATA.

###### 4.1.1. IATA key scheme (default):

The IATA centric key scheme is supposed to be used by airlines that primarily use IATA codes as airport
identifiers in their operations and planning processes. When this key scheme is used the interface uses IATA
code as primary key when storing airports in the JCMS model. Consequently, airports are also recognized by
other JCMS sub-systems by their IATA code. The following statements are true when the IATA key scheme is in
effect:

* Only airports with IATA code are stored
* Since the IATA code is used as key for airports, duplicate IATA codes is not supported in JCMS. However,
  several airports with the same IATA code may still exist in the standard Jeppesen airport feed. In order to
  resolve the occurrences of duplicate IATA codes in the feed, a configurable region preference (default set
  to North America) determines which airport instances to incorporate into the JCMS model (see [Handling of duplicate IATA codes](#stdif-airport-input-duplicate-iata-codes)).

###### 4.1.2. ICAO key scheme:

The ICAO centric key scheme is used by airlines that primarily use ICAO codes as airport identifiers in their
operations and planning processes. When this key scheme is used the interface uses ICAO code as primary key
when storing airports in the JCMS model. Consequently, airports are also recognized by other JCMS sub-systems
by their ICAO code. The following statements are true when the ICAO key scheme is in effect:

* Only airports with ICAO code are stored
* Duplicate ICAO codes is not supported. A new airport may however reuse the ICAO code of a closed airport.
  In such cases the identity of the old airport is taken over and its instance in the JCMS model is redefined
  by the new airport. The new airport may also reuse the IATA code of the old airport (if it exists), or else
  the IATA code is updated to match the new airport.

##### 4.2. Identification of objects

Data objects in the incoming airport data feed are identified by their *id* field. This is true for all
data types except airports which instead are instead identified as follows:

* In the standard Jeppesen airport feed airports are identified by their *iataCode* or *icaoCode* field,
  depending on which key scheme is used. IATA and ICAO codes are always stored in upper case.
* In a custom airport feed, airports are identified by their *extid* (external identifier) field
  (see [Handling of locally defined (custom) airport data](#stdif-airport-input-custom-airport-data)).

##### 4.3. Handling of closed airports

The standard Jeppesen airport feed is not only a snapshot of the currently existing airports, countries,
timezone data etc. Since it also carries a history of some of this data, the feed may contain airports that
have been taken out of service at some point in time. An airport that is just about to close may have a
validity period set in the feed that ends at some point in the near future, if a date for closure is known
in advance. The following statements are true regarding closed airports:

* The standard Jeppesen aiprot feed may contain closed airports.
* An airport in the feed is determined closed by the interface if the *created* timestamp in the root element
  of the import file is not enclosed by the most recent validity period of the airport.
* The interface marks an airport as closed by closing its validity period in the JCMS model.
* If a closed airport in the feed is not closed in the model, the interface updates any changes and closes it
  in the model. However there is an exception to this rule: since, in the ICAO centric key scheme, it is
  possible to reuse the ICAO code of a closed airport this means the interface must avoid closing the airport
  if it was reused by a previously processed (non-closed) instance in the feed.
* If a closed airport in the feed is already closed in the model, the interface leaves it unchanged in the
  model.
* If a closed airport doesn’t exist in the model, it is not created by the interface.
* If an airport is closed in the model but not in the feed it is updated according to the feed, i.e. after
  the update it is no longer closed in the model. This may occur if a new airport reuses the code of a closed one.
* Over time, the number of closed airports will increase. In order to limit the transfer of “dead” information,
  Jeppesen may choose to exclude airports from the standard airport feed, that were closed before a certain date.

##### 4.4. Handling of locally defined (custom) airport data

It is possible to add custom airports and other related objects locally in a JCMS model. These objects will
not be overwritten or touched by the interface as long as the identity of the custom object does not interfere
with any of the objects (of corresponding type) included in the standard feed.

Technically, the custom airport data is imported in the same way as the standard Jeppesen airport
data with the difference that the *source* attribute in the root element of the imported file must begin
with the word “custom”. All locally defined objects that are needed by a customer may be defined in the same
file. The file may be imported repeatedly and if any changes are made in the file since the last import,
this will be detected by the interface and the updates are applied to the JCMS data model. A typical use case
for locally defined objects is to add airports e.g. used for diversion, that are not included in the standard
Jeppesen airport feed. In the example below, an airport is added that doesn’t have neither an IATA nor ICAO
code. For custom airports, the identity is always specified in the *extid* (external identifier) field. As mentioned
above it is important to choose an identity that doesn’t collide with any existing IATA or ICAO code. Maximum 4
characters is allowed as airport identifier.

```
<?xml version='1.0' encoding='UTF-8'?>
<setAirportDataValidityRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AirportDataValidity/v2" version="2"
                               source="customAirportsXXX" created="2016-01-01T10:13:44" baseline="JAN2016.1.0" >
  <putAirport extid="00AK" name="Lowell Field" timeZoneProfile="America/Anchorage">
    <period validFrom="2016-01-01T00:00:00" country="US" subdiv="AK" latitude="215817" longitude="-546106"/>
  </putAirport>
</setAirportDataValidityRequest>
```

In this example the custom airport refers to e.g. a timezone profile that exists in the standard
Jeppesen feed. Therefore, the standard Jeppesen feed must be imported first, before applying the custom feed.
It would of course also be possible to define custom timezone profiles and other objects as needed, as long
as their *id* don’t collide with those in the standard Jeppesen feed.

##### 4.5. Handling of changed ICAO codes

An airport may change ICAO code if it changes country, since region/country is part of the semantics built in
to the ICAO code itself. If the IATA key scheme is in effect, the change of ICAO code is trivial. Since it’s
not used as key for the airport, the interface can simply update the ICAO code with the new value from the feed.
In the ICAO key scheme the interface creates a new copy of the airport using the new ICAO code as key. The old
instance is not removed by the interface since the airport may still be referenced by objects inside JCMS with
its old ICAO code. The old instance will however not be updated henceforth in case there are changes to the
airport in future feeds.

##### 4.6. Handling of changed IATA codes

In rare cases an airport may change IATA code. If the ICAO key scheme is in effect, the change of IATA code is
trivial. Since it’s not used as key for the airport, the interface can simply update the IATA code with the
new value from the feed. In the IATA key scheme the interface creates a new copy of the airport using the new
IATA code as key. The old instance is not removed by the interface since the airport may still be referenced
by objects inside JCMS with its old IATA code. The old instance will however not be updated henceforth in case
there are changes to the airport in future feeds.

##### 4.7. Handling of duplicate IATA codes

Duplicate IATA codes is not supported in JCMS when using the IATA key scheme, since the IATA code is used as key in the model.
However, some of the airport codes assigned by IATA are in fact duplicates and therefore duplicate IATA codes also exist in
the standard Jeppesen airport feed. In order to resolve the occurrences of duplicate IATA codes in the feed,
a configurable region preference (default set to North America) determines which airport instances to incorporate
into the JCMS model. The interface ignores airports with duplicate IATA code that don’t belong to any of the
preferred regions.

If, despite the region preference, there still exists airports with duplicate IATA codes (not counting airports
that are closed in the feed) then the interface keeps track of the duplicates as they appear when processing
the feed and takes the following actions:

> * The first instance encountered in the feed is identified and stored as it would normally do with any
>   non-duplicate airport, but subsequent duplicates are ignored.
> * At the end of processing, the interface issues a warning message in the log file listing all duplicates with their extid,
>   IATA and ICAO and region codes according to the data in the feed. The operator is then encouraged to
>   specify in the interface configuration the external id’s of the duplicates to ignore at future import
>   occasions. If such a configuration exists, the interface validates the configured external id’s agains
>   those in the feed, to double check that they still represent airports with duplicate IATA codes, before
>   updating the airport in the model. This is done in order to to avoid any inadvertent updates in case the
>   source system has changed external id’s of those airports in the feed.

##### 4.8. Configuration

**Airport key scheme**
:   Configures which code, IATA or ICAO, that is used as identifier for airports (see [Supported airport key schemes](#stdif-airport-input-airport-key-schemes))
    The default key scheme is IATA.

**Regional preference**
:   Sets the regional references to use for resolving Airports with duplicated IATA codes.
    In case of duplicates in the incoming feed, an Airport within any of the preferred regions is selected in
    favor of one that belongs to some other region.
    This setting is only relevant when using IATA as key scheme. The default preferred region is ‘NOA’ (North
    America).

**Ignored airports**
:   Defines list of airports to ignore by external id. The purpose of this configuration setting is to provide
    a more fine grained selection among airports with duplicate IATA codes. If e.g. two airports within the same
    region have the same IATA code in the incoming feed, the regional preference (see above) is not sufficient
    to narrow down which one of the duplicates to import into JCMS. The airports specified in this list will not
    be imported by the interface if they are duplicate IATA airports.
    This setting is only relevant when using IATA as key scheme. The list of ignored airports is empty by default.

##### 4.9. Error handling

The interface conforms to the same error handling strategy as most of the standard interfaces, i.e. to reject
the incoming message if it cannot be entirely and completely processed. In such cases one or more error
messages are also issued in the log file, containing detailed information about the error.

If the interface encounters several errors, all errors belonging to the same data entity are collected before
the processing is terminated.

Beside error messages, a number of warning messages may also appear in the log file. During processing of an
airport feed, warning messages may appear either in combination with error messages or without presence of
any error message. In the latter case, the entire feed was processed successfully, but the warning(s) indicate
that there may be anomalies that the operator should be aware of and possibly corrective actions need to be
taken. Below is a summary of the warning messages and possible corrective actions:

| Warning message | Cause and corrective actions |
| --- | --- |
| extid=’<..>’ in configured exclude list contains a non-duplicate airport with IATA code=’..’ | The configured list of ignored airports contains an airport without duplicate IATA code. Either due to misconfiguration or because extid’s have been rearranged in the source feed. Check the configured list of ignored airports and only include extid’s of airports that are reported as duplicates by the interface. |
| Unique match not found for airport with IATA=<..> and ICAO=<..>, skipping | There exists more than one airport with the same code (IATA or ICAO depending on key scheme). Either due to manipulation of the code in the data model from outside the interface, or a custom airport with an IATA/ICAO code that is already used as key in the standard Jeppesen feed. The operator should determine whether the anomaly is expected (a desired effect of data manipulation) or change back the code that is causing it. |
| Airport with ‘<..>’ as id already exists, will change ICAO code from ‘<..>’ to ‘<..>’. | The interface has detected that an airport in the feed has changed key but an airport already exists in the model having the new code as id. The purpose of the warning is to alert that the ICAO field of that airport will be changed. The root cause is either that the ICAO code has been manipulated in the data model from outside the interface, or that a new IATA duplicate has appeared in the standard feed. In the latter case an additional warning message about duplicate IATA codes is also issued. See “Duplicate IATA codes found…” for corrective actions. |
| Duplicate IATA codes found when handling request: <..> Airport with conflicting IATA code: <..>, extid=<..>, region=<..>, icaoCode=<..>, name=<..> | This warning indicates that, using the IATA key scheme, there are airports in the feed with duplicate IATA code(s) that cannot be resolved based on the configured region preference and ignored extid list. The region preferences and/or ignored extid list should be corrected and the feed should then be re- imported. |

##### 4.10. Use cases

###### 4.10.1. Add a custom airport

It is possible to add and update airport data that is not included in the standard Jeppesen airport feed,
by sending a custom airport feed through the Airport Data Input interface. The interface identifies an
input message as a custom feed by looking at the *source* attribute in the root tag. Any source starting
with ‘custom’ is determined as a custom airport feed. In a custom feed, airports are identified by the
*extid* field, as opposed to the standard Jeppesen feed where airports are identified by their IATA and/or
ICAO codes.

In the following example a custom airport is added by using a custom airport feed. The custom airport
is associated with a timezone, country and country subdivision that are all defined in the standard Jeppesen
airport feed. It is therefore assumed that a custom airport feed like this one is used as a complement
to the standard feed, and that the standard feed has been loaded into the JCMS system first, before
applying the custom airport feed.

```
<?xml version='1.0' encoding='UTF-8'?>
<setAirportDataValidityRequest xmlns="http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/AirportDataValidity/v2" version="2"
                               source="customAirportsXXX" created="2016-01-01T10:13:44" baseline="JAN2016.1.0" >
  <putAirport extid="00AK" name="Lowell Field" timeZoneProfile="America/Anchorage">
    <period validFrom="2016-01-01T00:00:00" country="US" subdiv="AK" latitude="215817" longitude="-546106"/>
  </putAirport>
</setAirportDataValidityRequest>
```

In the data model of JCMS, this will result in a new airport:

| id | name | icao | iata | tzprofile |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 00AK | Lowell Field |  |  | America/Anchorage |

,and its time dependent data defined in a separate entity (airport\_period):

| airport | validfrom | validto | city | country | subdiv | region | latitude | longitude |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 00AK | 1JAN2016 00:00 |  |  | US | AK |  | 215817 | -546106 |

### Airport Slot Management


This chapter describes the standard interfaces for automatic management of airport slots.
The scope of these interfaces is the Ops Control system.
At some airports an airport slot is needed for any flight to depart or arrive. A slot is to be
seen as a contract between the airline and the airport, giving the airline the right to arrive
at and depart from an airport at a certain time of day with a certain aircraft type. The slot grants the
arrival/departure of the flight(s) within a specific time window. Stepping away from the agreed terms
means that the airline needs to follow a procedure which involves asking for permission to make a change
and waiting for the response.

Airport slot management is used at airports where demand is higher than capacity, at least during certain
times during the day, as a means to avoid congestion. Slot managed airports have a function called slot
coordinator (or slot facilitator) responsible for coordinating slots and communicate with airlines and
other stakeholders. The communication between JCMS and the slot coordinator uses standardized messages
described in Chapter 6 in the IATA SSIM Manual.

The Ops Control system keeps an up to date state of existing airport slots within a certain time window (current day + 3).
The time window is related to the operational time window and thus moves forward as time passes.
It is the task of the airport slot management services to retrieve existing slots from the slot
coordinator for all slot managed airports that are used by flights within the current time window. It
also detects situations that require new slot clearance requests and follows up on the response of such
requests.

##### 5.1. Services

In JCMS, the following services are involved in the airport slot management process:

###### 5.1.1. Slot Requests Output

This service is responsible for generating slot messages, sent from airline to airport slot coordinators.
The service finds relevant slot managed airports in JCMS within current slot window and sends requests to
slot coordinators of those airports for all existing slots within the slot window.
This service also fulfills the task of initiating the importing of allocated airport slots, when no slot information
yet exists in JCMS. Therefore no separate initial loading of slot information is needed.

The service generates the following type of slot messages:

* **SIR-Q** (Slot Information Request Query):
  The service sends SIR request messages to all slot managed airports each 6 hours. A SIR-Q message requests all slots
  within the current slot window for a specific airport.
  The service use Consul as a registry for storing the slot window associated with each sent SIR requests.
* **SCR/SMA** (Slot Change Request):
  The service performs continuous analysis of all airport slots within the current slot window, identifying those requiring changes.
  SCR/SMA messages are then generated to airport coordinators for the concerned airport slots.
  An airport slot requires a change when associated flight leg in JCMS has significantly changed (for example changed aircraft type or number of seats).
  The business logic to determine whether a flight leg has significantly changed is airline specific and must be defined in the configuration layer, see [Rave definitions](#rave-definitions).
  The service also identifies airport slots where the associated flight leg has been cancelled, and no airport slot is required anymore.
  Slots without any associated flight legs are currently not analyzed and managed by this service.
  In terms of communication, SCR messages are generated for level 3 coordinated airports, whereas SMA messages are generated for level 2 coordinated airports.

####### 5.1.1.1. Inconsistent state

The interface identifies situations where a user has saved temporary or intermediate changes to the aircraft rosters that
affects one or more slots. Changes to the affected slots are deferred and not sent to the slot coordinator until the state
of the model is deemed consistent. In an inconsistent state one or more slot coordinated flight legs have typically been
deassigned from the aircraft, however the inconsistent state may comprise not only the slots that are directly affected by
deassigned legs but additional slots may be indirectly affected due to aircraft swaps involving several aircrafts.

###### 5.1.2. Slot Response Input

This service is responsible for processing slot messages sent by airport slot coordinators to the airline,
updating the slot information in JCMS accordingly.
When processing slot messages, the service first tries to look up existing slot records in JCMS matching the
received slot information. The status (action code) of existing slots records in JCMS are updated to reflect the
new received information. New slot records are created in JCMS if no matching slot records are found.
The service also match flight legs in JCMS with the departure / arrival information of the received slot information and
associates the matching legs with the slot record in JCMS. Slot records are created in JCMS even if no matching flight legs are found.

The service can process the following type of slot message:

* **SIR** (Slot Information Request):
  It’s assumed that information in the received SIR response message corresponds with the slot window for the latest sent SIR-Q message for respective airport.
  The service use Consul for looking up the latest requested SIR period and updates slot records in JCMS as a state,
  meaning that existing slots are removed from JCMS if not included in the SIR response being processed.
  Slots outside the latest requested SIR period are not processed or updated in JCMS.
  The service use Consul as a registry for storing information that SIR response has been received.
* **SCR/SMA** (Slot Change Request):
  Updates the status (Confirmation, Refusal, Cancellation, Offer, etc.) for airport slots in JCMS
  based on the information received from airport slot coordinator.

After consuming a message, the service also sends a message back to MRM in order to update MRM meta data about the slot message. Header property *‘mrm\_msg\_id’*
on the incoming message is used to reference the message to update in MRM. The meta data includes information about the addressed airport and the service consuming
the message along with any error or warning messages. For SCR/SMA messages the meta data also includes information about flights involved.

##### 5.2. Design

The slot management services are not defined using SMOG and thus no artifacts are built by the
IOService builder. Instead IOServer handlers and IOService configuration is provided in CARMSYS as
part of the Standard Interfaces component.

##### 5.3. Configuration

###### 5.3.1. Rave definitions

The following Rave variables are defined in the CARMSYS and used by the Airport Slot Management standard interface:

* `interfaces_core.%leg_requires_departure_slot_request%`: Returns true only when the flight leg requires a departure slot and the current slot associated with the flight leg departure must be changed though communication to airport coordinator with SCR/SMA message.
* `interfaces_core.%leg_requires_departure_turnslot_request%`: Returns true only when the flight leg requires a turn slot for departure and the current slot associated with the flight leg departure must be changed though communication to airport coordinator with SCR/SMA message.
* `interfaces_core.%leg_requires_arrival_slot_request%`: Returns true only when the flight leg requires an arrival slot for arrival and the current slot associated with the flight leg arrival must be changed though communication to airport coordinator with SCR/SMA message.
* `interfaces_core.%leg_requires_arrival_turnslot_request%`: Returns true only when the flight leg requires a turn slot for arrival and the current slot associated with the flight leg arrival must be changed though communication to airport coordinator with SCR/SMA message.

The business logic behind these Rave variables need to be implemented in a CARMUSR to comply with the
expected behavior of each individual airline.

###### 5.3.2. Configuration of IOServer

IOServer need to be configured for hosting the interface IOServices:

```
<include href="${CARMSYS}/etc/service_template/airport_slot_mgmt/AirportSlotRequests.xml" />
<include href="${CARMSYS}/etc/service_template/airport_slot_mgmt/AirportSlots.xml" />
```

The following queues must be included in ccf configuration, typically located at `$CARMUSR/etc/ccf.xml`:

```
<include href="${CARMSYS}/etc/ccf/airport_slot_mgmt.xml"/>
```

###### 5.3.3. Infrastructure

Airport slot messages are communicated by email. The Slot Requests Output IOService is configured to forward
messages to Message Recipient Management (MRM) where per airport subscriptions are created for distributing
messages to email addresses of respective airport slot coordinator. MRM is also set up to read a mailbox
reserved for response messages from airport slot coordinators, and route those messages to the
Slot Response Input IOService.

### API Hotels Integration


This chapter describes the interfaces that provides JCMS with an automated hotel accommodation process in cooperation with the external
crew accommodation provider Accommodations Plus International (API), providing airlines with services such as sourcing, negotiation, planning,
operations & logistics, billing and analytics.

##### 6.1. Overview of the business process

The integrated solution described here consists of a bidirectional exchange of information between JCT and the hotel booking system ACES from API.
It is designed to provide JCMS with a planned view of crew accommodations as well as responding to day of operation changes in order to keep the state of
hotel bookings automatically up-to-date and consistent with the actual air traffic situation, crew need etc. ACES always prioritizes responding to changes
to trips close to or on day of operation whereas changes to trips further out may be placed on queue to be picked up at a later date.

The data flowing in the direction from JCT to ACES serves the
purposes of communicating the need for hotel accommodation by sending the actual state of trips (pairings) and their assignments. When trips for the
upcoming planning period have been created in JCMS they are sent to ACES as a batch. Trips are completed with personal assignments as rosters are being
released for the various crew groups. Changes are then communicated to ACES in an on-event fashion, as the trips and rosters are maintained in JCMS.
In the same way, updates are also sent during the operational phase for assignment changes, flight cancellations, trip splits, flight delays and other
events that might affect the need for hotel accommodation or transportation to/from hotels or venues, as soon as changes are made in JCT. For the purpose
of booking local transportation to/from venues in ACES, venue information is included for ground tasks in the trip messages sent to ACES. Venue information
in this context is for example the location of a simulator or other training facilities.

The task of selecting actual hotels and room types based on the communicated need is essentially in the hands of ACES and is based on cost criteria,
availability as well as whatever other rules implemented in ACES for governing the choice of accommodation depending on crew, trip- or flight related properties.
It is the responsibility of ACES to fulfill the need for hotel accommodations at all times. However, JCT can also hint ACES about preferred hotels, specific
hotels requested by crew or special placeholders (so called *forced hotels*) for accommodation where a layover cannot be directly derived from the structure of
the trip, such as day rooms or need for hotel room at beginning or end of a trip. In addition to explicitly hinting ACES about the need for day rooms, ACES can
also be configured to automatically book day rooms for long stops.

JCT can also inform ACES about occasions where hotel or transport is not needed
for certain crew members due to private arrangements. Such arrangements may be initiated either from JCT or from ACES by means of the MyCrewCare mobile app.
In the latter case, information about declined hotel accommodation is sent over from ACES to JCT along with hotel bookings for the layover in question.

The data flow from ACES to JCT serves the purpose of providing JCMS with both a preliminary view of bookings as a response to the initial batch of
planned trips and to maintain an up-to-date state of bookings for JCMS as changes occur. Closer to day of operation, as roster assignments become available
and bookings are being confirmed by hotels, ACES sends confirmed personalized bookings to JCT. The communication around accommodation and transport need
as well as actual bookings is trip centric, i.e. both systems are using the trip concept as common planning object. As a consequence, so called non-crew
working on board the aircraft e.g. as technicians, air marshals or attending cargo, are normally not supported since they are not assigned to any of the
plannable crew positions of the trip. The trip name and IdentifierDate is used as a combined business key when trips are communicated between the systems.

Normally, all crew members on a certain trip have the same need for accommodation but it is not always the case.
Crew may be allocated different hotels e.g. for availability or contractual reasons.

Furthermore, despite the trip centric approach, individual crew requests as well as individual duty briefing times can still be communicated and taken into
account by ACES.

In addition to hotel rooms and local hotel/venue transportation, ACES can also create and maintain bookings for ground transport trip activities and send them
over to JCT. Furthermore there are also additional data feeds for keeping crew data, hotels, transport companies and other master data in synch between the
two systems. Hotels and transport companies and the associated contractual information is owned and mastered by ACES whereas crew and master data such as
bases, airports, duty codes and crew positions are mastered by JCT.

###### 6.1.1. Synchronization of trips and bookings

There are two booking periods maintained in ACES, the current period containing trips that are currently being operated and a future period containing the planned
trips. The booking periods may align with the bid periods used at the airline. Another option is to use a rolling time window, for example 28 days, to define the
booking periods.

Trips and hotel bookings are always synchronized between JCT and ACES for the current booking period. Following steps describe how the next booking period is
planned and maintained. The exact process might differ for individual airlines, but the steps gives an idea of what a typical process could look like.

1. Trips for next booking period are available in JCT. When and how trips are imported to JCT is airline specific and is not further described in this document.
2. Trips are exported from JCT and loaded into ACES for the next booking period. All trips are loaded to ACES as a batch, providing the total layover need that is to be planned. This step is typically done about 20 days before the next booking period and can either be triggered manually or automatically from JCT.
3. Planning is performed in ACES and hotels are assigned to the trips for the booking period. This step typically takes 5 days to finalize.
4. Hotel bookings are automatically sent from ACES to JCT for the planned trips. The trips in JCT now have information of hotels booked for each layover.
5. Crew are assigned to trips in JCT as part of the bidding / rostering process.
6. Trips with crew assignments are exported from JCT to ACES for the next booking period. All trips are sent to ACES as a batch. This step is typically done about 7 days before start of next booking period. All changes to these trips are automatically sent from JCT to ACES after this point in time for keeping the booking period up to date.
7. The booking period is maintained in ACES to match the trips and crew assignments received from JCT. Hotel bookings are updated in ACES and automatically communicated back to JCT. The picture below illustrates how trips and hotel bookings are synchronized between JCT and ACES for the next booking period at different points in time.

![../_images/ACES_trip_synchronization.png](../_images/ACES_trip_synchronization.png)

##### 6.2. Design overview

###### 6.2.1. Interfaces

The guiding design principle is that the two systems, JCT and ACES, should be loosely coupled and operate independently. Operations in the sending system should
not be affected if the receiving system is unable to handle or receive the sent messages. A number of interfaces is used for integrating the two systems:

![../_images/api_hotels_overview.png](../_images/api_hotels_overview.png)

Communication between the systems is asynchronous and stateless, where messages are exchanged in a publish/subscribe fashion. The responsibility of a
publishing system is to send messages on agreed channels. The responsibility of the subscribing system is to receive and handle the messages accordingly.
The receiving system is responsible for error handling related to the received messages. The two systems (ACES and JCT) can use API and Jeppesen infrastructure
for direct communication, but it is also possible to route the communication via the airlines infrastructure.

####### 6.2.1.1. A1 Crew Info

The purpose of this interface is to keep ACES updated with the list of employees (crew members) for which hotel accommodations are managed. Non-crew are not included.
Crew data sent to ACES consist of crew member id (employee number), first and last name, gender, employments, home bases, aircraft qualifications, groups, positions
and hide periods.

Except from the crew member id, name and gender, all other record types sent over this interface come with a time validity, i.e. they can vary in time. For this kind
of data JCT tracks changes and stores the complete timeline i.e. current as well as historical and future data (if available). However the timeline sent to ACES
over this interface is by default limited to the current and next planning periods, i.e. from beginning of the current planning period until the end of the next
planning period.

The service produces messages on an internal interface format and then transforms them to the external ACES format by means of an xslt transformation (see [Schemas, services and operations](#stdif-api-hotels-schemas)).

######## 6.2.1.1.1. Hide periods

Hide periods are the combined periods of hold periods and unacknowledged periods for the crew member. This is communicated to ACES in order not to disclose information to crew
,e.g. from the MyCrewCare mobile app, about any assignments that may only be preliminary. In order for ACES to be able to react immediately to changes in hide periods,
e.g. as a result of crew acknowledging a roster change, crew data is sent on event-basis for crew as soon as there is a change in their hide periods.
In a customer installation, the Crew Info feed is also set up to run in a batch fashion in order to keep the rest of the crew data up-to-date and to make ACES aware
of any new crew members.

######## 6.2.1.1.2. Translation of aircraft qualifications

Aircraft qualifications extracted from JCT are translated into fleet codes used by ACES. Since fleet codes in ACES are maximum 3 characters the aircraft qualifications
are by default translated into fleet codes by simply taking the 3 first characters of the qualification type code. This translation may need to be customized since
the naming scheme for qualification type codes may differ between airlines. Override method **get\_qual\_id** of class **std\_interfaces.api\_hotels\_1.CrewDataInterfaceHandler**
in order to extract a custom fleet code based on an aircraft qualification.
Aircraft qualifications in JCT are recognized as crew qualifications having category code “aircraft”.

####### 6.2.1.2. A2 Planned Pairings

The purpose of this interface is to export trips from JCT and load into ACES for the next booking period. All trips are loaded to ACES as a batch,
providing the total layover need that is to be planned. The feed comes in two flavors with similar content, the ‘*Load-Pairings*’ and the ‘*Update-Pairings*’ message
which both have very similar schema. When trips are initially created in JCMS, before they are known to ACES, JCT sends a Load-Pairings batch to ACES containing
the trips in open time. When rosters have been assigned, JCT sends an ‘*Update-Pairings*’ batch with the assigned trips. In a customer installation, the
Planned Pairings feed is set up to run in a batch fashion either by automatically scheduled jobs at certain dates of the month or to be manually initiated.

A trip must meet the following criteria to be sent to ACES:

* trip is not cancelled
* trip has a crew complement
* trip contains at least one activity
* trip is not a wrapper trip (category = ‘PRIV\_TASK’) containing only one activity

The service produces messages on an internal interface format and then transforms them to the external ACES format by means of an xslt transformation (see [Schemas, services and operations](#stdif-api-hotels-schemas)).

######## 6.2.1.2.1. Special layover requests

Normally, API Hotels derives the need for accommodation based on the state of the trips and makes reservations according to booking rules in ACES. However, this
interface is also able to convey various requests along with the trips. ACES will use such requests as input in the booking process and try to accommodate them
if possible. Note that the types of special requests listed here also apply to interface **A3 Pairing/Roster Updates**. As an example, if a request for a certain
hotel has been placed on a trip, that request is included in the trip *state* and thus included in (A2 or A3) messages to ACES, containing that trip.

Requests may be on trip level or roster level. Trip level requests apply to all crew/positions of the trip, whereas roster level requests only apply to specified
crew members. Trip level requests may be combined with roster level requests either to make exceptions to a trip level request for certain crew member(s), or to
add properties to a trip level request for individual crew member(s). As an example, a hotel specified in a trip level request is overridden by another hotel
for a certain crew member as specified in a roster level request. See also [Use cases](#stdif-api-hotels-use-cases) for an example of a trip level request.

| Type of request | Level | Data model | plan\_event\_type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Request for a specific hotel for a layover. For trip level requests, requested hotel can also be retrieved from Rave variable *interfaces\_core.%requested\_hotel\_id\_after\_duty%*. | trip/roster | trip\_event / roster\_event / Rave | HOTEL\_OVERRIDE |
| Request for a layover before the first duty of the trip. May be combined with a request for a specific hotel (see above). If not, it indicates a “placeholder” for an accommodation where ACES is free to select hotel. | trip/roster | trip/event / roster\_event | FORCED\_HOTEL |
| Request for a layover after the last duty of the trip. May be combined with a request for a specific hotel (see above). If not, it indicates a “placeholder” for an accommodation where ACES is free to select hotel. | trip/roster | trip\_event / roster\_event | FORCED\_HOTEL |
| Request for a dayroom, i.e. a need for accommodation between two activities in a duty. May be combined with a request for a specific hotel. If not, it indicates a “placeholder” for an accommodation where ACES is free to select hotel. A dayroom request may be issued independently from any built-in rules for booking dayrooms that may exist in ACES. | trip/roster | trip\_event / roster\_event | FORCED\_HOTEL |
| Decline accommodation on a regular layover. | roster | roster\_event | SKIP\_ROOM |
| Decline accommodation on a layover before the first duty of the trip (as specified by trip level request). | roster | roster\_event | SKIP\_ROOM |
| Decline accommodation on a layover after the last duty of the trip (as specified by trip level request). | roster | roster\_event | SKIP\_ROOM |
| Decline dayroom (as specified by trip level request). | roster | roster\_event | SKIP\_ROOM |
| Decline transportation to and/or from hotel on a layover before the first duty of the trip (as specified by trip level request). | roster | roster\_event | SKIP\_TO\_HOTEL / SKIP\_FROM\_HOTEL |
| Decline transportation to and/or from hotel on a layover after the last duty of the trip (as specified by trip level request). | roster | roster\_event | SKIP\_TO\_HOTEL / SKIP\_FROM\_HOTEL |

In addition to the plan\_event\_type codes above, the interfaces also recognizes the code ‘NO\_HOTEL’ which means both room and transports are declined. In the case
where decline of accommodation is initiated from ACES (by means of the MyCrewCare app), the A6 interface does not distinguish between decline of room vs. transports.
Therefore one **roster\_event** of each type (SKIP\_ROOM, SKIP\_TO\_HOTEL and SKIP\_FROM\_HOTEL) is created. See also [Handling of declined hotel accommodations](#stdif-api-hotels-declined-hotel).

######## 6.2.1.2.2. Message header attributes

The following headers attributes are attached to each message sent over interfaces A2 and A3:

**current\_pp** - Set to ‘True’ if the message contains trips with *IdentifierDate* that are within the range of the current planning period, else ‘False’.

**next\_pp** - Set to ‘True’ if the message contains trips with *IdentifierDate* that are within the range of the next planning period, else ‘False’.

A planning period ‘pp’ is defined as the period between two points in time tStart and tEnd, i.e. tStart <= t < tEnd.

The logic to determine if a trip *IdentifierDate* ‘d’ is within the range of a planning period ‘pp’ is to compare ‘d’ with the date part of tStart and tEnd, i.e.
date(tStart) <= d <date(tEnd).

Example 1,
Message containing trips with *IdentifierDate* between 1NOV2020 and 1DEC2020
current planning period: 1OCT2020 00:00 - 1NOV2020 00:00
next planning period: 1NOV2020 00:00 - 1DEC2020 0:00
result: ‘current\_pp’ = ‘False’, ‘next\_pp’ = ‘True’

Example 2,
Message containing trips with *IdentifierDate* between 1FEB2020 and 28FEB2020
current planning period: 1FEB2020 08:00 - 1MAR2020 08:00
next planning period: 1MAR2020 08:00 - 1APR2020 08:00
result: ‘current\_pp’ = ‘True’, ‘next\_pp’ = ‘False’

Example 3,
Message containing trips with *IdentifierDate* between 1FEB2020 and 15MAR2020
current planning period: 1FEB2020 08:00 - 1MAR2020 08:00
next planning period: 1MAR2020 08:00 - 1APR2020 08:00
result: ‘current\_pp’ = ‘True’, ‘next\_pp’ = ‘True’

######## 6.2.1.2.3. Deadheads and Sick Transports

Information whether a flight leg is used by the airline for positioning crew due to deadheading or sick transport, is forwarded to ACES to allow for business logic
with special considerations or arrangements.

####### 6.2.1.3. A3 Pairing/Roster Updates

The purpose of this interface is to keep ACES up to date with changes to trips and their activities (segments) and assigned crew, close to and during day of operation.
Changed trips are identified by a trigger service in JCT and sent with their new state, one message per trip. Although conceptually different from the batch feeds
described above in [A2 Planned Pairings](#stdif-api-hotels-planned-pairings), the trip state information sent for a trip is the same.

The following types of changes are picked up by the trigger:

* trip split operations
* trip slice operations
* new trips
* removed trips
* cancelled trips
* activities added to trip
* activities removed from trip
* changes to duty overrides
* schedule time or venue changes of ground activities
* changes of scheduled, estimated or actual times of flights
* changes to hotel requests both on trip and on the individual crew level
* changes to crew declines of hotel accommodations and transports
* changes to forced hotels both on trip level and for individual crew members
* changes to briefing time overrides both on trip level and for individual crew members
* changes in aircraft assignments
* trips becoming released for crew members
* changes to crew-trip assignments

In addition to these trip related changes, the trigger also identifies situations where a trip that is de-assigned from a roster overlaps another trip on the same
roster. In this case both trips are sent to ACES regardless if the latter trip is subject to any of the above changes or not.

Messages are not sent for changes to trips in historic time. By default, changes to trips ending more than 5 days ago are not sent. Furthermore, the trip must meet
the following criteria to be sent to ACES:

* trip is not cancelled
* trip has a crew complement
* trip contains at least one activity
* trip is not a wrapper trip (category = ‘PRIV\_TASK’) containing only one activity

The service produces messages on an internal interface format and then transforms them to the external ACES format by means of an xslt transformation (see also [Schemas, services and operations](#stdif-api-hotels-schemas)).
The trigger picks up changes at discrete times following the so called model refresh interval in the IOServer. The trigger creates a ‘TripEventsMsg’ message on the
internal interface format containing all changes in one change-set, i.e. changes that occurred since the last model refresh. The ‘TripEventsMsg’ is then transformed
into multiple messages on the external ACES formats.

######## 6.2.1.3.1. Event messages sent to ACES

There are specific messages sent for trip cancellations ‘*Delete-Pairing*’, assignment changes ‘*Assign-Pairing*’, and new trips ‘*Add-Pairing*’. All other events
are communicated using the ‘*Revise-Pairing*’ message. For trip slice and split operations, the ‘*Revise-Pairing*’ message contains both trips resulting from the
operation. If a trip is subject to several changes, more than one of these message types may be sent. The interface then guarantees that the messages are sent in
a logical order. The ‘*Add-Pairing*’ and ‘*Revise-Pairing*’ messages contain the full state of the trip including their crew assignments. Therefore if e.g. a trip
has been created and assigned in the same transaction then the ‘*Assign-Pairing*’ is redundant and only the ‘*Add-Pairing*’ message is sent.
For the ‘*Assign-Pairing*’ message, even though it only contains the trip key and crew assignments, always contains the full state of assignments. I.e. if a crew
member has been de-assigned from a trip, the message contains all the remaining crew assignments. See [Schemas, services and operations](#stdif-api-hotels-schemas) for the schemas of these messages.

######## 6.2.1.3.2. Message header attributes

The following headers attributes are attached to each message sent over interfaces A2 and A3:

**current\_pp** - Set to ‘True’ if the message contains trips with *IdentifierDate* that are within the range of the current planning period, else ‘False’.

**next\_pp** - Set to ‘True’ if the message contains trips with *IdentifierDate* that are within the range of the next planning period, else ‘False’.

A planning period ‘pp’ is defined as the period between two points in time tStart and tEnd, i.e. tStart <= t < tEnd.

The logic to determine if a trip *IdentifierDate* ‘d’ is within the range of a planning period ‘pp’ is to compare ‘d’ with the date part of tStart and tEnd, i.e.
date(tStart) <= d <date(tEnd).

Note that the ‘*Revise-Pairing*’ message is also sent as a response to a ‘*Request-Pairing-Refresh*’ message sent by ACES to query for trip state of individual
trips (see [A4 Request Pairing Request](#stdif-api-hotels-request-pairing-request)).

######## 6.2.1.3.3. Incident lock

An incident lock flag, that a flight leg may be tagged with in JCT, is forwarded to ACES in order for API Hotels to restrict access to information related to such
a flight leg.

######## 6.2.1.3.4. Deadheads and Sick Transports

Information whether a flight leg is used by the airline for positioning crew due to deadheading or sick transport, is forwarded to ACES to allow for business logic
with special considerations or arrangements.

######## 6.2.1.3.5. Additional duty information

By adding a Hotel Option comment on a certain layover in a trip, a crew tracker in JCT can convey information about special arrangements to ACES. Such information
and arrangements are agreed between the airline and API Hotels on a project implementation basis. An example could be special pickup locations for charter flights.
The information is stored in JCT as a **trip\_event** of type **HOTEL\_OVERRIDE** and transferred by the interface as a duty remark. Should more than one such trip\_event
exist for the same trip layover, all comments are concatenated and comma-separated into one duty remark.

####### 6.2.1.4. A4 Request Pairing Request

The purpose of this interface is to give ACES the possibility to query JCT for the current trip state for individual trips or all trips within a period.
It is mainly used for recovering from out-of-synch issues that may occur due to outages, missed messages etc, but can also be useful when testing
the system integration. Communication is asynchronous, where a request message is published from ACES to JCT and a response message is published back from
JCT to ACES on interface A3 Pairing/Roster Updates or A2 Planned Pairings depending on request type (see below).

Request messages are sent on an external ACES format and transformed into an internal format by means of an xslt transformation. Response messages are also
produced on an internal interface format and transformed into the external ACES format. See also [Schemas, services and operations](#stdif-api-hotels-schemas) for more information.
Depending on the request type, JCT responds with different types of response messages:

* Request type “list-of-pairings” yields one or more messages of type *Revise-Pairing* (see [A3 Pairing/Roster Updates](#stdif-api-hotels-pairing-roster-updates))
* Request type “range-request” yields one message of type *Update-Pairings* (see [A2 Planned Pairings](#stdif-api-hotels-planned-pairings))
* Request type “list-of-bases” is ignored by JCT.

####### 6.2.1.5. A5 Hotel Data Export

The purpose of this interface is to load and update JCT with information about hotels and transportation companies (TC) used for accommodating and transporting
crew members on layovers. This information is needed in JCMS primarily for crew control to know how to contact crew on the layover. The list of hotels and TCs
are also used in JCT for crew trackers to select hotels when requesting specific hotels. The information (including rates and other hotel contract details) may
also be used by the pairing/tracking optimizers for finding overall optimal scheduling solutions.

In a customer installation, the Hotel Data Export feed is normally set up to run in a batch fashion on a nightly basis. As a complement, the feed may also be set
up to run on an event basis, exporting new or modified hotels or TCs as soon as they are added/modified in ACES. If e.g. a hotel booking is received for a hotel
that is not yet known to JCT, the hotel is created ad-hoc with temporary limited information. The information about the hotel is then limited to name,
address and phone number until the hotel becomes available in the Hotel Data Export feed. The interface also creates a record in **airport\_hotel** associating
the layover station with the newly created hotel.

Only hotels and transportation companies included in a message from ACES are created/updated in JCT. Hotels and transport companies that exist in JCT but are
not included in the feed are not deleted in JCT by the interface. JCT is informed about hotels and transportation companies no longer in use through the validity
period of their contracts.

Messages are sent on an external ACES format and transformed into an internal format by means of an xslt transformation (see also [Schemas, services and operations](#stdif-api-hotels-schemas)).

####### 6.2.1.6. A6 Pairing Hotel Details

The purpose of this interface is to keep JCMS up to date with information about what hotels and transports that are planned/booked/confirmed for each layover and crew
member. This information is required in JCMS primarily for crew control to know that all crew have accommodations and transports for the layovers and how crew can be
contacted if needed, but also for crew members to know what hotels and transport companies that have been allocated for them.

Messages are sent on an external ACES format and transformed into an internal format by means of an xslt transformation (see also [Schemas, services and operations](#stdif-api-hotels-schemas)).

The information sent over this interface is trip centric i.e. hotel and transport bookings are reported and managed per trip. One or more trips can be reported per
message and for each trip the complete state of bookings are always reported. This means for a certain trip bookings are always included for all layovers and all
positions of the trip. A consequence of the trip centric approach is also that ACES sends new booking status also in cases where trips are sliced or split without
changing the actual need for accommodations. As an example, slicing a trip results in a part of the booking need being shifted from the original trip to the new
resulting trip. While the total booking need remains the same (and thus the hotel reservations remain unchanged), there is a change in the state of bookings seen
from the trip perspective, therefore ACES must report the new booking states for the original trip and the new resulting trip.

The interface supports the following functional features:

* anonymous bookings (for open positions)
* personal bookings (for assigned crew members)
* crew members split to multiple hotels on the same layover
* bookings for layover before first duty of the trip
* bookings for layover after last duty of the trip
* dayroom bookings
* booking status per individual hotel reservations
* multi-night layovers
* multiple venue transport bookings during multi-night layovers to/from hotel
* information about crew members with declined hotel
* check-in/out times
* transport pickup times

######## 6.2.1.6.1. Matching of existing booking records

Because ACES sends the complete state of bookings for a trip, in many situations the message will contain information that has not changed compared to the state
of bookings already in JCT. In order to cause as few updates as possible, the interface identifies what differs and updates only those records in the JCT database.

When receiving reservations for a certain trip layover from ACES, the interface first tries to match the given start and end times of the layover with the trip’s
Rave calculated duty start and end times, or activity start/end times in case of dayrooms (in this context it should also be pointed out that reservations for
multi-night layovers span over more than one duty). These duty (or activity) times must match exactly. If a match is not found, the default
behaviour in JCT is to ignore the reservation. It can generally be assumed that such mismatches are of temporary nature and are caused by trips being rebuilt in
JCT or by considerable delays of flights. When the trip has been updated in ACES, the new booking state sent should then match the trip in JCT.

If the reservation is deemed to match the trip, the interface tries to find an existing **hotel\_booking** record to reuse. It first looks among previously handled
bookings to see if there is an exact match that can be reused. An exact match is one that matches not only start/end times, station and hotel but also transport
companies, booking status, check-in/out and pickup times. This is the case when ACES reports the same layover in separate <layover> or <accomodation> elements for
different crew members.

If no candidate was found the interface then tries to find an existing **hotel\_booking** record that best matches the given hotel reservation. It is checked that the
selected candidate has not already been associated with some other reservation in the message. If a matching record is still not found a new **hotel\_booking** is
created.

Based on the **hotel\_booking** record, the interface then tries to find an existing **trip\_event** record to reuse (or one per layover night in case of multi-night
layover), first among the **trip\_event** records referencing the **hotel\_booking** record and secondly among other **trip\_event** records associated with the trip.
If no match is found a new **trip\_event** record is created with a reference to the **hotel\_booking** record.

When booking records have been created/updated as needed, personal bookings are matched and created if needed for any crew members associated with the reservation
from ACES. Any obsolete **crew\_hotel\_booking** records are deleted (as needed e.g. following a crew swap). Also the *cnt* and *grouped\_cnt* columns of the
**hotel\_booking** are updated to reflect the booked crew members.

######## 6.2.1.6.2. Handling of intermediate booking states

An intermediate booking state arises in the JCT data model when a change has been done in JCT that will affect the (trip centric) view of bookings, but JCT has
not yet received reservations from ACES that reflect the new state. Some operations, e.g. slicing or splitting a trip, may leave previously confirmed
bookings with an undefined status, in the intermediate booking state. The interface can detect this situation when a **hotel\_booking** record is handled, by looking at
the trip(s) referencing that **hotel\_booking**. If it is no longer referenced by the trip it was once created for, it indicates that the original trip has been split. The interface
then updates the **hotel\_booking** status to “**New**” indicating that a new state update from ACES is pending. Note that the column *booking\_ref* holds a “soft
reference” to the trip for which the booking was created. This value of *booking\_ref* remains for as long as the intermediate booking state lasts. In the “final”
booking state, after receiving notifications from ACES that reflect the new state, *booking\_ref* refers to the new trip segment.

In the case of slicing a trip, all **trip\_event** records refering to the original trip are cloned and the new clones are associated with the new trip slice.
This happens as an integral part of the slice operation in JCT and leaves the data model in an intermediate state where the existing booking records are referenced
both from the original trip and the new trip slice. In this case the interface clones the **hotel\_booking** records so that each booking is only referenced from
one **trip\_event**. The booking status is set to “**New**” for the booking records associated with a trip for which notifications has not yet arrived from ACES.

For more information see ‘Splitting and slicing a trip’ in [Use cases](#stdif-api-hotels-use-cases).

######## 6.2.1.6.3. Handling of cancelled bookings

ACES does not support sending cancelled bookings. However when an updated booking state is received from ACES, any non-matching **hotel\_booking** records that may
exist already in the JCT database are updated with status “CANCELLED”. This way bookings are implicitly cancelled in JCT. Any **trip\_event** records referencing
the cancelled **hotel\_booking** records are deleted, unless they also belong to another trip. Any **crew\_hotel\_booking** records referencing the cancelled
**hotel\_booking** are also removed.

######## 6.2.1.6.4. Handling of declined hotel accommodations

In the case where decline of accommodation is initiated from ACES (by means of the MyCrewCare app), the interface does not distinguish between decline of room vs.
transports. Therefore one **roster\_event** of each type (SKIP\_ROOM, SKIP\_TO\_HOTEL and SKIP\_FROM\_HOTEL) is created. The interface also adds ‘EXT API Hotels’ as
remark in order to distinguish them from declines initiated from JCT. This is important in order for the interface to correctly identify the case where a previous
decline in MyCrewCare has been removed, and thus to prevent the interface from removing **roster\_event** records initiated from JCT, e.g. created in the Tracking
Editor.

####### 6.2.1.7. A7 Request Hotel Request

The purpose of this interface is to give JCT the possibility to query ACES for the current state of hotel and transport bookings.
It may be used for recovering from out-of-synch issues e.g. due to outages, missed messages etc, but can also be useful when testing
the system integration. Communication is asynchronous, where a request message is published from JCT to ACES and a response message is published back from
ACES to JCT on interface A6 Pairing Hotel Details. There are two types of requests available, by trip or by roster (by specifying employee number and period).

Request messages are sent on an external ACES format. Response messages are produced on an external ACES format and transformed into the internal interface
format. See also [Schemas, services and operations](#stdif-api-hotels-schemas) for more information.

This interface is available on a configuration basis, if deemed necessary by a customer implementation project. There is no built-in feature in JCT for issuing
request messages of this kind.

####### 6.2.1.8. A8 Transport Bookings

The purpose of this interface is to keep JCT up to date with booking information for ground transportations between airports/cities made in ACES.
Ground transportations, for example taxi or limo activities, are sent to ACES as trip duty ground segment activities on interface [A2 Planned Pairings](#stdif-api-hotels-planned-pairings) or
[A3 Pairing/Roster Updates](#stdif-api-hotels-pairing-roster-updates). API Hotels may arrange the bookings of such ground transports and send transport booking details back to JCT.
The transport booking details is primarily required in JCMS for crew members to know what transport company that provides the transport.

Booking messages are sent from ACES when transport bookings are created or updated. Messages are sent on an external ACES format and transformed into an internal
format by means of an xslt transformation (see also [Schemas, services and operations](#stdif-api-hotels-schemas)).
The internal interface is the same as the one used for hotel bookings (see [A6 Pairing Hotel Details](#stdif-api-hotels-pairing-hotel-details)).

For each booking, the interface creates a public annotation on the ground transport activity in the JCMS data model, containing the name and phone number of the
transport provider. The correct ground transport activity object is found by matching the given start and end stations, and ‘fuzzy’ matching of the given start and
end times against existing ground transports assigned to the given trip. If several candidates are found within the allowed deviation (default 60 minutes), the one
closest in time is picked. The interface writes ‘EXT API Hotels’ in the *‘created\_by’* field of the annotation in order to recognize it as a ground transport booking
annotation, in case there are other public annotations associated with a certain ground transport. If a ground transport booking annotation already exists, the
interface updates the annotation text and the *‘creation\_time’* if the provider name or phone number has changed.

####### 6.2.1.9. J1 Static Data

The purpose of this interface is to simplify and standardize the import of static data from JCT into ACES and keep the static data in ACES up to date with changes
in JCT. This interface consists of two feeds for different types of static data (a.k.a. master data or catalog data), the ‘AirportDataValidity’ and the
‘CatalogDataOutput’. In a customer installation, the ‘CatalogDataOutput’ feed is typically set up to run in a batch fashion once per night whereas the latest
version of the airport data is always available as an xml file to download from Jeppesen Plaza.

The ‘AirportDataValidity’ message contains the following types of master data:

* airports
* time zones
* daylight saving time patterns
* cities
* countries
* country subdivisions
* regions

The ‘CatalogDataOutput’ message contains the following types of master data:

* airlines
* crew bases
* crew groups and categories
* qualification groups and categories
* seniority groups
* planning periods
* activity (duty) types, groups and categories
* aircraft types, groups and body types
* flight service types
* currencies
* coterminals
* trip categories
* gender codes

Note that for this interface there doesn’t exist any external ACES format. ACES consumes Jeppesen interface formats for these feeds (see also [Schemas, services and operations](#stdif-api-hotels-schemas)).
For more details on these feeds please see [Airport Data Input](airport_input.html#stdif-airport-input) and [Catalog data output](catalog_data_output.html#stdif-catalog).

| A7 (response) | [LayoverInput\_1.xsd](contract/api_hotels_1/LayoverInput_1.xsd) | CrewOnTripHotel | setLayovers | from\_pairing\_hotel\_details.xsl | [Pairing-Hotel-Details-JCTE.xsd](contract/external/schema/Pairing-Hotel-Details-JCTE.xsd) |
| A8 | [LayoverInput\_1.xsd](contract/api_hotels_1/LayoverInput_1.xsd) | LayoverInput | setGroundTransportDetails | from\_GTNotification.xsl | [GTNotification-JCTE.xsd](contract/external/schema/GTNotification-JCTE.xsd) |
| J1 | [CatalogDataOutput\_1\_beta.xsd](contract/std_interfaces.catalog_data_output_1/CatalogDataOutput_1_beta.xsd) | CatalogDataOutput | getAllCatalogData |  |  |
| J1 (airport data) | [AirportDataValidity\_2.xsd](contract/std_interfaces.airport_input_2/AirportDataValidity_2.xsd) | AirportDataValidity | setAirportDataValidity |  |  |

###### 6.2.3. Data Model

The picture below shows the portion of the JCMS data model most relevant for the API Hotels Integration. Details have been left out for clarity and only primary key
columns and selected external references have been included. Please refer to the UDM documentation for more details. Also see [Use cases](#stdif-api-hotels-use-cases) for
examples of how the data model is used by the interfaces.

As can be seen from the picture, there are actually two tables that can hold hotel and transport bookings - **trip\_event** and **hotel\_booking**.
While **hotel\_booking** reflects the actual bookings as received from ACES, **trip\_event** represents a “best known” state of bookings which means either an “intended”
hotel allocation or the actual bookings. There are also other uses for the **trip\_event** table in the context of hotel bookings, e.g. to indicate “forced hotels” or
requests for specific hotel. The type of **trip\_event** is determined by the referenced **plan\_event\_type**.

The **trip\_event** records always represent a single layover night on a certain trip. Multi-night layovers are mapped to several **trip\_event** records, one per night,
but only one **hotel\_booking record** (see also [Multi-night layovers](#stdif-api-hotels-multi-night-layovers)). The individual **trip\_event** records therefore reference the same
**hotel\_booking**, which then covers the total multi-night layover length.
There may also be more than one instance of **trip\_event**/**hotel\_booking** per layover night e.g. in case crew are split up on different hotels or different transport
companies. In those cases the *grouped\_cnt* shows number of crew and positions for each booking.

In contrast to **trip\_event**, **roster\_event** never represent bookings. In the context of hotel bookings it is only used to indicate “forced hotels”, requests
for specific hotel or declined hotel or transport for individual crew members. Personal hotel and transport bookings are represented by the **crew\_hotel\_booking**
table.

The dashed line from **hotel\_booking** to **trip** in the figure represents a “soft reference” to the trip for which the booking was created, stored in column *booking\_ref*.

![../_images/hotel_data_model.png](../_images/hotel_data_model.png)

###### 6.2.4. Booking statuses

The following booking status codes are used in the API Hotels integration.

| JCT status | ACES status | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BOOKED | BOOKED | Booking is confirmed. |
| CANCELLED | CANCELLED | Booking is cancelled. |
| PENDING\_CONFIRM | PENDING CONFIRMATION | Rooms have been reserved but not confirmed by hotel. |
| PENDING\_CANCEL | PENDING CANCELLATION | Cancellation is initiated but has not been confirmed by the hotel. |
| New |  | Booking is in an intermediate state. This status is initiated from JCT, there is no corresponding corresponding status sent by ACES. |

The interface can be configured to ignore certain booking statuses from ACES. By default, status codes “PENDING CANCELLATION” and “CANCELLED” are ignored by JCT.
For more information about cancelled bookings and the *New* status see [Handling of cancelled bookings](#stdif-api-hotels-cancelled-bookings) and [Handling of intermediate booking states](#stdif-api-hotels-intermediate-booking-states).

###### 6.2.5. Multi-night layovers

Multi-night layovers are represented by several **trip\_event** records, one per night, but only one **hotel\_booking** record. However multi-night bookings may also be
associated with multiple transportations to/from hotel or venues in which case more than one **hotel\_booking** record is needed in order to correctly model all
associated transports. In this case all of the **hotel\_booking** records have the same start/end time reflecting the total length of the multi-night layover.

The first layover night is assumed to have a transport from airport to hotel whereas the last layover night is assumed to have an associated transport from hotel to
airport. In case of multiple transports, intermediate layover nights may also have transports from venue to hotel and/or from hotel to venue.
A venue is for example the location of a simulator or other training facilities associated with a ground duty. Based on the specified transport pickup times the
interface tries to associate each transport with the correct layover.

##### 6.3. Configuration

###### 6.3.1. IOService builder and IOServer configuration

The following IOService builder configuration is needed for building the services used by the API Hotels integration:

```
<ioservice name="CrewOnTripHotel_1_event_plainxml" pattern="trigger" handler_module="std_interfaces.triggers.api_hotels_trip_events" >
  <description>Output trips to API Hotels, on-event updates.</description>
  <smog-service name="CrewOnTripHotel" version="1" protocol="plainxml">
    <service-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/services_crew_on_trip.xml"/>
    <protocol-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/protocol.xml"/>
    <service-mapping location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/mapping_crew_on_trip_event.xml"/>
  </smog-service>
</ioservice>

<ioservice name="CrewOnTripHotel_1_requested_plainxml" pattern="requestresponse">
  <description>Output trips to API Hotels, batch feed.</description>
  <smog-service name="CrewOnTripHotel" version="1" protocol="plainxml">
    <service-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/services_crew_on_trip.xml"/>
    <protocol-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/protocol.xml"/>
    <service-mapping location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/mapping_crew_on_trip_requested.xml"/>
  </smog-service>
</ioservice>

<ioservice name="CrewDataHotel_1_event_plainxml" pattern="trigger" handler_module="std_interfaces.triggers.api_hotels_crew_changes">
  <description>Crew data to API Hotels, on-event updates.</description>
  <smog-service name="CrewDataHotel" version="1" protocol="plainxml">
    <service-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/services_crew_info.xml"/>
    <protocol-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/protocol.xml"/>
    <service-mapping location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/mapping_crew_info_event.xml"/>

<ioservice name="CrewDataHotel_1_requested_plainxml" pattern="requestresponse">

</ioservice>

<ioservice pattern="subscriber">

    <service-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/services_layover_input.xml"/>
    <protocol-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/protocol.xml"/>
    <service-mapping location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/mapping_layover_input.xml"/>
  </smog-service>
</ioservice>

<ioservice pattern="subscriber">
  <description>Hotels and Transportation company master data from API Hotels.</description>
  <smog-service name="HotelInfo" version="1" protocol="plainxml">
    <service-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/services_hotel_info.xml"/>
    <protocol-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/protocol.xml"/>
    <service-mapping location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/mapping_hotel_info.xml"/>
  </smog-service>
</ioservice>

<ioservice pattern="requestresponse">
  <description>Service for extracting static catalog data.</description>
  <smog-service name="CatalogDataOutput" version="1.beta" protocol="plainxml">

    <protocol-spec location="$CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/std_interfaces.catalog_data_output_1/protocol.xml"/>
```

is currently not included in OTS.

| A2,A4 | CrewOnTripHotel | CrewOnTripHotel\_1\_requested\_plainxml.xml | $CARMUSR/etc/programs/ioservice\_batch.xml |
| A3 | CrewOnTripHotel | CrewOnTripHotel\_1\_event\_plainxml.xml | $CARMUSR/etc/programs/ioservice\_single1.xml |
